META.subject: Physics
META.subtitleDoc: CBE Phenomenon-Driven Lesson Sequence — Sub-Strand 3.3 (7 Lessons)

UNIT.subject: Physics
UNIT.content:
• Conductors, insulators, semiconductors and superconductors
• Intrinsic semiconductors
• Extrinsic semiconductors (n-type and p-type) and doping
• Effect of temperature on the conductivity of materials
• Superconductors and their applications (e.g. MRI magnets)
• Applications of semiconductors and superconductors in solar panels, microchips and ICT devices
UNIT.learningOutcomes:
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) classify materials as conductors, insulators, semiconductors and superconductors based on their electrical properties,
b) describe intrinsic and extrinsic (n-type and p-type) semiconductors,
c) explain how doping and temperature change the conductivity of semiconductors,
d) explain the special properties and uses of superconductors,
e) relate the properties of these materials to their applications in household wiring, solar panels, microchips and MRI machines,
f) appreciate the role of electronics in Kenya's technological growth and renewable energy.
UNIT.coreCompetencies:
• Critical thinking and problem solving: the learner compares materials, analyses evidence on conductivity and temperature, and explains why each material suits its application.
• Communication and collaboration: the learner works in groups to test materials, discuss findings and present explanations of the energy band and doping models.
• Digital literacy: the learner uses the PhET simulation to investigate semiconductors and doping.
• Learning to learn: the learner revises a cumulative model of conduction as new evidence is gathered across the lessons.
UNIT.values:
• Responsibility: the learner handles electrical materials, wires and any liquid nitrogen demonstration safely and uses electrical devices responsibly.
• Unity: the learner cooperates in groups to carry out investigations and build shared models.
• Integrity: the learner reports observations honestly, even when they differ from predictions.
UNIT.sep:
• Asking questions and defining problems: students generate questions for the Driving Question Board about why materials differ in conductivity.
• Developing and using models: students build and revise particle and energy-band models of conductors, insulators, semiconductors and superconductors.
• Planning and carrying out investigations: students test copper, glass, wood, plastic and a diode for conduction.
• Analyzing and interpreting data: students interpret conductivity-temperature trends.
• Constructing explanations: students explain household wiring, solar cells and MRI magnets using evidence.
• Obtaining, evaluating and communicating information: students analyse case studies of solar panels, microchips and superconducting magnets.
UNIT.pcis:
• Safety and security: safe handling of electrical wiring and insulation to prevent shocks and fires in homes and workshops.
• Environmental education: use of solar energy as a clean renewable energy source.
• Education for sustainable development: promoting renewable energy and proper disposal of electronic waste (e-waste).
UNIT.careers:
• Electrical technician or electrician: choosing conductors and insulators for safe wiring in homes.
• Solar installation technician (e.g. in Kisumu, Kitui or Garissa): installing and maintaining solar PV systems.
• Electronics and ICT engineer: designing circuits and microchips for phones and computers.
• Biomedical engineer or radiographer: operating MRI machines at hospitals such as Kenyatta National Hospital.
• Materials scientist or physicist: researching new semiconductors and superconductors.
UNIT.focus: This unit helps learners explain why materials differ in how they carry electric current and how this is used in wiring, solar panels, microchips and MRI machines. Learners predict, test and model conduction, build up from conductors and insulators to semiconductors, doping and superconductors, and finally apply their ideas to Kenyan renewable energy and technology cases.
UNIT.phenomenon: In a Kenyan home in Nairobi, the electrician wires a house with copper cable covered in plastic. Copper carries electricity efficiently, while the plastic covering, wood and glass do not, so a person can safely hold the insulated wire while it carries current. Students test copper wire, glass, wood, plastic and a diode chip in a simple circuit and see a bulb light only for some of them, with the diode conducting in one direction only. It is puzzling because all these materials are made of atoms with electrons, yet they behave so differently. Why do metals like copper carry current easily while plastic and wood do not, and what makes the semiconductor in between so useful?
UNIT.supportingPhenomena:
• Semiconductors in solar cells and microchips control the flow of electricity, e.g. in solar panels on rooftops in Kenya and in mobile phones.
• Adding small amounts of impurities (doping) changes the conductivity of semiconductors.
• Conductors become less efficient at higher temperatures, semiconductors become more conductive, and superconductors lose all resistance below a critical temperature.
• Superconducting magnets in MRI machines produce strong magnetic fields without energy loss.
• Plastic, rubber and glass insulators prevent unwanted current flow and protect users.
UNIT.drivingQuestion:
DRIVING QUESTION: Why do some materials conduct electricity while others do not, and how does this affect the safety and efficiency of household wiring and of devices such as solar panels, computers and MRI machines?

KICD KEY INQUIRY QUESTIONS:
1. How do semiconductors and superconductors differ from ordinary conductors and insulators?
2. How is electronics applied in day-to-day life?
UNIT.storylineThread:
Lesson 1: Students predict which materials (copper, glass, wood, plastic, a diode) will light a bulb, test them, and start the Driving Question Board and a first model of conduction.
Lesson 2: Students classify conductors, insulators and semiconductors, link the classification to household wiring safety and the role of insulators, and revise the model.
Lesson 3: Students investigate intrinsic semiconductors (silicon, germanium) and explain why they conduct a little and how temperature increases their conductivity.
Lesson 4: Students explain doping to make extrinsic n-type and p-type semiconductors and why doping makes semiconductors useful in electronics.
Lesson 5: Students use the PhET simulation to explore conductivity, doping and energy bands, and test and refine their models with digital evidence.
Lesson 6: Students examine superconductors, critical temperature and zero resistance (with a liquid nitrogen demonstration or video if possible), and explain superconducting MRI magnets.
Lesson 7: Students analyse case studies of solar panels, microchips and superconducting magnets in Kenya's technological growth, finalise their models and answer the Driving Question.

LESSONS.title: Which Materials Light the Bulb? Launching the Phenomenon
LESSONS.duration: 40 minutes (one double or one single lesson; if single, run Observe and Explain in 25 minutes and keep DQB and Model to 15 minutes)
LESSONS.aresKeywords: conductor, insulator, semiconductor, diode, free electrons, Driving Question Board (DQB), class model, forward-biased, reverse-biased

slo.purpose: To launch the anchoring phenomenon: Mr Otieno, an electrician in Nairobi, wires a house with copper cable covered in PVC plastic and safely holds the insulated wire while it carries current. Learners predict, test and compare materials in a simple circuit, discover that only some materials let current flow, and begin to ask why.
slo.knowledge: Materials differ in whether they let current flow. In the test circuit, copper lights the bulb brightly, while glass, dry wood and plastic do not. A silicon diode lights the bulb in one direction only (forward-biased: lit; reverse-biased: off). So 1 of 4 ordinary materials conducts. All the materials are made of atoms with electrons, which raises the puzzle of why they behave so differently.
slo.skills: Making and justifying predictions (NGSS SEP: Asking Questions and Defining Problems); planning and carrying out a fair test in a circuit with a fixed test order (SEP: Planning and Carrying Out Investigations); recording and organising observations in a table (SEP: Analyzing and Interpreting Data); drawing a first model of electrons in materials (SEP: Developing and Using Models); communication and collaboration in groups.
slo.attitudes: Curiosity about why materials behave differently; respect for peers' ideas and open-mindedness when predictions turn out wrong; responsibility when handling dry cells, clips and wires; appreciation of the work of electricians such as Mr Otieno and of electronics in day-to-day life.
slo.keyInquiry: 1. How do semiconductors and superconductors differ from ordinary conductors and insulators? 2. How is electronics applied in day-to-day life? (Launched today, answered across Lessons 2 to 7.)
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 1 launches the phenomenon and the unit. It builds on nothing earlier. Learners gather first-hand evidence from the five-material test (copper, glass, dry wood, plastic, diode), start the Driving Question Board (DQB) with their own questions, and draw a first class model of electrons and atoms. Later lessons revise this model: Lesson 2 classifies materials by resistivity, Lesson 3 explains pure semiconductors, Lesson 4 doping, Lesson 5 tests band models with a simulation, Lesson 6 superconductors and MRI, Lesson 7 the final answer.
slo.safetyNotes: Use only two 1.5 V dry cells in series (3 V) and a 3 V torch bulb; never connect to mains (240 V) sockets. Do not short-circuit the cells with copper wire: keep the copper in the gap only briefly (a few seconds) and disconnect after each reading because the wire and clips may warm. Handle the glass piece with care (use a smooth-edged piece or rod; report any chips). Connect the 1N4007 diode with correct orientation and do not leave it connected for long. Keep liquids and water away from the circuit. Wash hands after handling cable insulation offcuts. Teacher must check every circuit before learners close it.

LESSONS.overview: Ms Achieng opens with the image of Mr Otieno wiring a Nairobi house with copper cable covered in PVC plastic, holding the insulated wire while it carries current at 240 V. She asks learners what makes that safe. Learners predict which of five materials (copper, glass, dry wood, plastic, diode) will light a 3 V bulb in a simple circuit and explain why. In groups, like Wanjiku and Kamau, they test the materials in the fixed order and record results: copper lights the bulb brightly; glass, dry wood and plastic do not; the diode lights the bulb forward-biased and not reverse-biased. In the Explain phase, learners compare predictions to evidence, note that only 1 of 4 ordinary materials conducts, and that the diode behaves differently from all of them. They name the puzzle: all materials are made of atoms with electrons, yet behave so differently. They then write questions for the Driving Question Board (DQB) and draw a first class model of electrons in a conductor and in an insulator, which will be revised in every later lesson. Lesson 1 does not explain energy gaps or resistivity; those come later.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners look at a picture or the teacher's description of Mr Otieno, an electrician in Nairobi, wiring a house with copper cable covered in PVC plastic and holding the insulated wire safely while it carries current. Individually, then in pairs, they complete a prediction table for the five materials in the fixed order (copper wire, glass, dry wood, plastic strip, silicon diode): Will the bulb light? Yes / No / Only one way. Beside each prediction they write one reason ('I think this because...'). For the diode they sketch how they might connect it and predict whether direction matters. Pairs then share predictions with a neighbouring pair.
framework.teacherMoves: Show the image and say: 'Mr Otieno is holding a wire carrying 240 V and he is not hurt. What do you notice about the wire?' WAIT TIME 10 seconds before taking answers. Say: 'Today we will test materials in a very safe 3 V circuit. Before we test, I want your prediction and your reason. There are no wrong predictions today.' Hold up each material in the fixed order. Give 3 minutes for silent individual prediction, then 3 minutes pair talk. Cold-call 3 pairs: 'What did you predict for wood, and what is your reason?' Then ask: 'Who predicted differently?' and cold-call 2 more. Record the class tally on the board (for each material: number predicting yes, no, one way) without saying who is right. Ask: 'What do you think happens with the diode if we flip it around?' and WAIT TIME 10 seconds.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (POE) with a public class tally. Committing to a prediction and a reason, in writing, exposes learners' initial ideas (for example 'wood is natural so it conducts' or 'all metals and all plastics behave alike'). Because the tally is recorded before testing, learners later feel the surprise or confirmation of the evidence, which motivates the need for an explanation.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that 100% of learners have written a prediction and a reason for all five materials (walk round with a checklist). Listen for reasoning types: appeals to appearance ('shiny'), to everyday use ('wires are covered in plastic'), or to particles ('electrons move'). Note at least 5 learners whose reasons mention a particle idea or everyday safe use of wire and whose ideas you can call on later. Record the class tally as baseline data.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of 4 (roles: circuit builder, tester, recorder, reporter), learners build the test circuit: two 1.5 V dry cells in series (3 V), a 3 V torch bulb and crocodile clips, leaving a gap in the circuit. First they close the gap with a clip-to-clip touch to check that the bulb works. Then they test the materials in the fixed order: (1) copper wire 10 cm, (2) glass rod/piece, (3) dry wood (ordinary ruler/stick), (4) plastic strip (stripped cable insulation), (5) silicon diode (1N4007), first forward-connected, then reversed. They record in a table whether the bulb is bright, off or lit, and also note anything else, such as the wire feeling warm. Like Wanjiku and Kamau, they compare results with their predictions. Expected results: copper, bulb bright; glass, off; wood, off; plastic, off; diode forward-connected, lit; diode reverse-connected, off.
framework.teacherMoves: Demonstrate the safety rules first: 'Cells and bulb only. Never touch these clips to a socket. Disconnect after each reading.' Check each circuit before groups test anything: 'Hands up when your bulb lights with the clips touching, and I will come to check.' Circulate and ask: 'What does the bulb tell you about the current?' and 'What would you expect to see if the current were very small?' Remind groups to keep to the fixed order. When groups reach the diode say: 'Test it, then reverse it. Tell me exactly what you see each time.' WAIT TIME 10 seconds after posing 'Why might the diode behave differently from the copper?' without answering it. Cold-call 4 reporters to give one result each in the fixed order and write the class results on the board. Resolve any odd result (for example a dull bulb with a flat cell) by asking the group to retest rather than dismissing it.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured data collection with a shared class results table. A fixed test order and a common circuit let all groups produce comparable evidence, and pooling results lets learners see patterns (1 of 4 ordinary materials conducts) and an anomaly (the diode conducts one way only). Highlighting the diode as an anomaly generates real questions rather than teacher-given ones.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe whether groups: (a) build a working circuit and check it with touching clips, (b) test in the fixed order, (c) record bright/off for each material and both diode directions accurately, (d) disconnect after each reading. Collect recorded tables: at least 80% of groups should record copper bright, glass off, wood off, plastic off, diode lit one way and off the other. Note groups who record the diode result in words such as 'works only one way' or who spontaneously ask why.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners compare the class results with the prediction tally and discuss in groups: Which predictions were correct? Which surprised us? They state the pattern in a claim-evidence-reasoning frame: 'Claim: only copper lets current flow easily. Evidence: the bulb lit brightly with copper but stayed off with glass, wood and plastic.' They note that 1 of 4 ordinary materials conducts, and that the diode conducts in one direction only (forward-biased: lit; reverse-biased: off). They link back to Mr Otieno: the copper core carries current and the plastic (PVC) cover does not, which is why he can hold the insulated wire. Then they name the puzzle: all of these materials are made of atoms with electrons, yet they behave so differently. In pairs they write one 'I wonder' about why. Learners use the words conductor and insulator for the first four materials, and the term diode for the fifth, but not yet explain why.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at the board. Compare our results with our predictions. What stands out?' WAIT TIME 15 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners for a pattern, then 2 more for a surprise. Push for evidence: 'What did you see that tells you that?' and 'How do you know the bulb is off because of the material, and not a flat cell?' (point to the touching-clips check). Introduce the vocabulary: 'We call materials that let current flow easily conductors, and materials that almost do not let current flow insulators. We say almost none, not zero.' Return to the phenomenon: 'Mr Otieno holds the insulated wire. Which of our materials is the copper and which is the cover? What does our test say about why this is safe?' Cold-call 2 learners. Then pose the puzzle: 'Everything we tested is made of atoms, and atoms have electrons. So why do copper and plastic behave so differently? And what is going on with the diode, which seems to be in between?' WAIT TIME 15 seconds, then let pairs talk for 2 minutes. Do NOT give the energy-gap or resistivity explanation; say 'That is exactly what we will find out in the coming lessons.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) with explicit comparison of predictions to data. Writing claims tied to specific bulb observations stops learners from relying on appearance or assumption. Naming the puzzle (same building blocks, different behaviour) creates a need to know that drives the unit, and the diode anomaly signals that the conductor/insulator split is not the whole story.
framework.formativeAssessment: Listen for claims that cite specific evidence (for example 'copper bright, plastic off'). Check that learners distinguish conductor/insulator vocabulary from observation and that they use 'almost no current' rather than 'no electricity at all'. Look for at least 6 'I wonder' statements that go beyond 'what is the diode?' to particle ideas (for example 'do electrons move in copper but not in plastic?'). Note any misconception, such as 'plastic has no electrons' or 'wood is a conductor because it is natural', and record it for the DQB and for later lessons.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners write their questions on sticky notes or paper strips (one question per note) and post them on the class DQB under the heading of the Driving Question: Why do some materials conduct electricity while others do not, and how does this affect the safety and efficiency of household wiring and of devices such as solar panels, computers and MRI machines? Questions come from their predictions, results and 'I wonder' statements. In groups they cluster questions into categories (for example: why copper conducts; why plastic, glass and wood do not; what the diode is and why it works one way; how this links to solar panels, phones and computers; what MRI machines have to do with it). Each group reads out one question it most wants answered. Learners also copy the two KICD key inquiry questions onto the DQB.
framework.teacherMoves: Post the Driving Question and the two key inquiry questions at the top of the board. Say: 'Write every question you have, one per note. Good questions begin with why or how.' Give 4 minutes. Model one: 'Why can Mr Otieno touch plastic-covered wire but not bare copper?' Collect and cluster with learners: 'Who has a question that is like this one? Come and place it here.' Cold-call 4 learners to read and place a question. Ask: 'Which question could we answer by testing something? Which need us to learn more about what is inside the materials?' WAIT TIME 10 seconds. Tell learners: 'We will return to this board in every lesson and move notes to Answered as our evidence grows.' Ensure questions about solar panels, computers, M-Pesa phones and MRI machines at Kenyatta National Hospital are on the board, adding one yourself if none appears.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board (DQB) as a public record of learners' own questions. Clustering questions shows learners how their wonderings connect to one big question, gives them ownership of the unit, and creates a visible tracker to return to for questions answered, revised or new in Lessons 2 to 7.
framework.formativeAssessment: Count questions: aim for at least 2 per group, with at least 3 questions in the whole class about why the materials differ at the particle level and at least 2 about applications (solar panels, phones, MRI). Check that clusters are sensible and that quieter learners have contributed at least one note. Record frequent question types to plan which later lessons to emphasise.

framework.learnerExperience: On A4 paper or in their exercise books, learners draw a first model to explain why copper lets current flow but plastic (the PVC cover) does not. They draw a small piece of copper and a small piece of plastic, show atoms and electrons in each in any way they choose, and use arrows or labels to show where electrons move or do not move when the 3 V cells are connected. They add a third box for the diode with a question mark and a note: 'one way only – we do not know why yet'. They write a one-sentence 'what my model says' and one 'what my model cannot explain yet'. Groups combine their drawings on a large class model poster by agreeing on common features and marking disagreements with question marks (for example, do all electrons move, or only some?). The class model is pinned beside the DQB.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Use only what you have seen today. Draw what might be happening inside copper and inside plastic. It is fine to be unsure.' Circulate and ask: 'What does the arrow show? Why did you draw the electrons there?' and 'How does your model explain the bulb lighting with copper? How does it explain the bulb staying off with plastic?' Do not correct models; instead ask 'What evidence supports that?' Cold-call 3 groups to show their drawings, and ask the class: 'What do these models have in common? Where do they differ?' WAIT TIME 10 seconds. Build the class model poster from agreed features and write the disagreements as question marks. Close by saying: 'This is our first class model. In each lesson we will test it and revise it with new evidence.' Link to home: 'At home, look at a cable or extension lead. Which part is copper and which is plastic? Bring a question to add to the DQB.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Initial model construction and public comparison of models. Putting ideas about electrons and atoms into a drawing makes thinking visible, reveals alternative ideas, and gives learners something concrete to test and revise. Recording what the model cannot yet explain (the diode, the difference between copper and plastic) sets up the revision cycle across the unit.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for models that (a) show copper and plastic differently, (b) include electrons in both materials, (c) show some link between electron movement and the bulb lighting, and (d) acknowledge the diode as unexplained. Accept varied drawings. Note models that claim plastic has no electrons or that electrons are used up in the bulb; flag them to revisit, not to correct now. Check that each learner can state one thing the model explains and one thing it cannot.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, review: (1) Did learners commit to written predictions with reasons before testing, and what were the most common ideas (appearance, use, particles)? (2) Did all groups obtain the fixed results (copper bright; glass, wood, plastic off; diode lit forward, off reverse)? If not, was it a flat cell, a loose clip or the wrong diode orientation? (3) Which learners used the word 'electrons' unprompted, and which held misconceptions such as 'plastic has no electrons'? (4) Did the DQB contain questions on both particle-level explanations and real applications (solar panels, phones, MRI at Kenyatta National Hospital)? (5) Did I resist explaining energy gaps and resistivity early, leaving them for later lessons? Use the DQB clusters and the first class model to decide which questions to emphasise in Lesson 2, where learners classify materials by resistivity.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We tested copper wire, glass, dry wood, plastic and a silicon diode in a 3 V circuit with a torch bulb. The bulb was bright with copper, and off with glass, dry wood and plastic. With the diode connected forward (forward-biased) the bulb lit, and with it reversed (reverse-biased) the bulb was off. So 1 of 4 ordinary materials conducts, and the diode conducts in one direction only.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Materials differ in whether they let current flow: copper is a conductor, while glass, wood and plastic are insulators that let almost no current through, which is why Mr Otieno can safely hold plastic-covered copper cable. The diode is different from both groups because it depends on direction.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: We cannot yet explain why copper lets current flow and plastic does not, even though both are made of atoms with electrons, or why the diode works one way only. Our first class model shows electrons in each material, but it cannot explain these differences yet. Our DQB questions will guide what we investigate next.

LESSONS.title: Classifying Conductors, Insulators and Semiconductors
LESSONS.aresKeywords: conductor, insulator, semiconductor, resistivity, conductivity, ohm metre, copper, PVC, household wiring, 240 V, class model, Driving Question Board (DQB)

slo.purpose: Learners use resistivity data to classify materials as conductors, insulators or semiconductors and explain why copper cable covered in PVC makes Kenyan household wiring both efficient and safe.
slo.knowledge: Materials are classified by resistivity (rho, in ohm metre) at about 20 C. Order from lowest to highest: copper 1.7 x 10^-8, germanium 0.46, silicon (pure) 2.3 x 10^3, dry wood about 10^8 to 10^11, glass about 10^10 to 10^14, PVC about 10^13 or more. Conductivity is 1/rho. Copper is a conductor; glass, wood and PVC are insulators that allow almost no current; silicon and germanium are semiconductors with resistivity in between. Silicon is about 1.4 x 10^11 times more resistive than copper. In Mr Otieno's wiring (2.5 mm squared copper, PVC insulation, mains 240 V, 50 Hz) the copper carries current efficiently and the PVC keeps the current inside the wire so a person can hold the insulated cable safely.
slo.skills: Analysing and interpreting data (ordering resistivity values across many powers of ten); constructing classifications from evidence; using mathematics (powers of ten, ratios, 1/rho); developing and revising models; constructing explanations that link properties to safety.
slo.attitudes: Responsibility for electrical safety at home; curiosity about why materials behave so differently; respect for peers' ideas during discussion; appreciation of the skill of electricians such as Mr Otieno.
slo.keyInquiry: How do semiconductors and superconductors differ from ordinary conductors and insulators? (Focus: ordinary conductors, insulators and semiconductors.) How is electronics applied in day-to-day life? (Focus: household wiring.)
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 1 gave the class the five-material test (copper bright; glass, dry wood and plastic off; diode lit forward and off in reverse) and the first class model of electrons. This lesson turns those yes/no results into a quantitative classification using resistivity and links it to Mr Otieno's wiring. It also leaves open WHY the resistivities differ so much (energy bands, taken up later) and pushes the class toward the semiconductor question taken up in Lesson 3.
slo.safetyNotes: Do not experiment with mains electricity (240 V) in class; all circuit work uses the 3 V supply (two 1.5 V dry cells). Keep dry cells away from heat and do not short-circuit them with crocodile clips or copper wire for more than a moment because wires and cells can get hot. Remind learners never to touch damaged or exposed household cable or sockets and never to use wet hands near electrical appliances. Report cracked insulation to an adult.

LESSONS.overview: Ms Achieng opens by revisiting the Lesson 1 results: in the 3 V test circuit only copper lit the bulb, while glass, dry wood and plastic did not, and the diode conducted one way only. Learners predict how Mr Otieno's copper-and-PVC cable in a Nairobi house stays safe at 240 V, and where wood, glass and silicon would rank in a list from best to worst conductor. In the Observe phase, groups quickly re-run the fixed test (copper, glass, wood, plastic, diode) and then receive a resistivity data card (copper 1.7 x 10^-8, germanium 0.46, silicon 2.3 x 10^3, dry wood about 10^8 to 10^11, glass about 10^10 to 10^14, PVC about 10^13 or more ohm metre). They order the materials, notice the huge gaps between powers of ten, calculate that silicon is about 1.4 x 10^11 times more resistive than copper, and sort the materials into conductor, semiconductor and insulator. In the Explain phase they use the data to explain why household wiring uses copper covered in PVC, and why insulators allow almost no current rather than none. They add new questions to the DQB and revise the class model with a resistivity scale and a note that the reason for the differences is still unexplained.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall the Lesson 1 results (copper lit the bulb; glass, dry wood and plastic did not; the diode conducted one way). Individually they write and sketch a prediction in their notebooks: (a) Rank copper, glass, dry wood, plastic and silicon from best to worst at letting current flow, and (b) Mr Otieno holds the PVC-covered copper cable carrying current in a Nairobi house at 240 V. Why is he safe? They then compare predictions with a partner and star where they disagree. Wanjiku predicts that wood is the 'second best' because 'it comes from living things', while Kamau predicts silicon will be near copper. Learners are invited to treat these as ideas to test.
framework.teacherMoves: Project the Lesson 1 results table and say: 'Last lesson our bulb told us yes or no. Today we ask: how much better is copper than glass, and where does silicon fit?' Give 3 minutes of silent writing, then say: 'Rank the five materials and explain Mr Otieno's safety using the word electrons.' WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds of silence after posing the question before any talk. Pair-share for 2 minutes. Cold-call 4 pairs: 'Which material did you put last, and why?' Record ALL rankings on the board without judging. Ask: 'Who ranked differently from this pair? What was your reasoning?' Circulate and note learners who think insulators have exactly zero conduction or that thick wires matter more than material.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Eliciting prior ideas through a Predict-Explain-Compare routine. Making predictions public exposes ranking ideas and preconceptions (for example, wood is a better conductor than glass, or insulators conduct nothing at all) so that later data can confirm or challenge them, which builds learners' ownership of the revision.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe whether predictions include a ranking with a reason (not just a list). Look for: (1) copper placed first by at least 80% of learners; (2) use of electrons in explanations; (3) learners who connect the PVC cover to stopping current reaching the hand. Tally the misconceptions heard (for example, 'insulators have no electrons', 'silicon is the same as copper') on a sticky note to revisit in the Explain phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Part A (10 minutes): In groups of four, learners re-run the Lesson 1 test circuit (3 V from two 1.5 V dry cells, 3 V torch bulb, crocodile clips) in the fixed order: copper wire 10 cm (bulb bright), glass piece (off), dry wood ruler or stick (off), plastic strip from stripped cable insulation (off), silicon diode 1N4007 forward-connected (lit) and reverse-connected (off). They record bulb status in a table. Part B (20 minutes): Each group receives a resistivity data card with values at about 20 C in ohm metre: copper 1.7 x 10^-8; germanium 0.46; silicon (pure) 2.3 x 10^3; dry wood about 10^8 to 10^11; glass about 10^10 to 10^14; PVC about 10^13 or more. They (1) cut and arrange cards on a number line of powers of ten from lowest to highest rho, (2) calculate conductivity 1/rho for copper (about 6 x 10^7 per ohm metre) and for silicon (about 4 x 10^-4), and (3) calculate how many times silicon is more resistive than copper (2.3 x 10^3 divided by 1.7 x 10^-8, about 1.4 x 10^11). They then sort materials into three columns: conductor, semiconductor, insulator. They compare their order with their Predict ranking and mark where it changed.
framework.teacherMoves: Brief safety reminder: 'We only use our 3 V cells. We never test with the mains at home or in school.' Ask groups to assign roles: tester, recorder, reporter, safety checker. Say: 'Predict first: will the bulb light? Thumbs up or down. Then test.' Circulate and ask: 'Which material did the bulb tell you is a conductor? Does the bulb tell you how good a conductor?' Hand out the data cards after Part A and say: 'The bulb only says yes or no. Scientists measure resistivity to say how much.' Point to the number line: 'Look at the gap between copper and germanium, and between silicon and wood. What do you notice?' WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds after the question. Cold-call 3 groups to state their order. Ask: 'Why is the bulb dark for dry wood although wood is not infinite in resistivity?' (Guide: the current is too small to light the bulb, but not exactly zero.) Challenge: 'Each step on your number line is a factor of ten. How many steps from copper to PVC?' (More than 20.)
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data patterns and scale reasoning: ordering values across many powers of ten and calculating the ratio of silicon to copper gives learners a concrete sense of how huge the differences are. Sorting into three columns is a classification activity in which learners build categories from evidence (the numbers themselves) instead of memorising a definition, so the classification becomes a conclusion supported by the data.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check the recorded table matches the fixed results: copper bright; glass, wood and plastic off; diode forward lit and reverse off. Check the number line order is copper, germanium, silicon, wood, glass and PVC. Check that learners calculate about 1.4 x 10^11 and state it in words. Look for learners sorting copper under conductor, germanium and silicon under semiconductor, and wood, glass and PVC under insulator. Listen for the statement 'almost no current' rather than 'no current'.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners work in their groups to build a claim-evidence-reasoning (CER) explanation for the phenomenon: 'Why does Mr Otieno use copper cable covered in PVC for the sockets in a Nairobi house?' Claim: copper is a conductor and PVC is an insulator. Evidence: resistivity values (copper 1.7 x 10^-8 ohm metre; PVC about 10^13 or more ohm metre), the bulb results from the test circuit, and the 1.4 x 10^11 comparison for silicon. Reasoning: current flows easily through copper (low rho, less energy wasted as heat in the 2.5 mm squared cable), while PVC allows almost no current so the current stays in the wire, even at 240 V, and a person holding the insulated cable does not get a dangerous current. Learners also explain what silicon being in between means and why it is neither a good wire nor a good cover. They discuss the safety case: damaged PVC insulation, wet hands (water with salts reduces the protection), and why Kenyan homes use copper rather than dry wood or glass for wires. Each group writes one open question they cannot yet answer (for example, 'Why is copper's resistivity so low, and why do glass and PVC have such high resistivity when all are made of atoms?').
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Use the sentence frame: I claim ___ because the data show ___, which means ___.' Give 5 minutes of group writing. Cold-call 4 groups, one at a time: 'Read your claim and evidence.' After each, ask the others: 'What evidence would you add or challenge?' WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds before each reply. Press for precision: 'You said insulators do not conduct. What does the resistivity of PVC (about 10^13) tell us about that word? Say it with almost.' Probe: 'If copper is such a good conductor, why not wear it as a cover for the wire?' (Guide: the current would pass through the person.) Ask: 'Why is a bulb dark with wood even though wood is not at the very top of the list?' Return to the Predict misconceptions: 'Who changed their ranking? What data changed your mind?' Also ask: 'Our data tell us WHAT is different. Do they tell us WHY? What do we still need to explain?' Record the open questions to move to the DQB. Do not give the energy band explanation yet.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) with whole-class critique. Structuring the explanation forces learners to connect numerical evidence to the safety phenomenon, and peer challenge strengthens reasoning. Naming what the data cannot yet explain (why resistivities differ) creates a purposeful gap that motivates later lessons on energy bands and semiconductors.
framework.formativeAssessment: Use a 3-point rubric on the CER: (1) claim uses the terms conductor and insulator correctly; (2) evidence quotes at least two resistivity values with units (ohm metre); (3) reasoning links low rho to efficient current flow in copper and high rho to safety in PVC and uses almost no current. Look for a learner who explains that silicon is a semiconductor with resistivity in between and cannot be used as either wire or cover. Collect one exit ticket sentence: 'PVC keeps Mr Otieno safe because ___.'

framework.learnerExperience: Learners go to the class DQB and (1) review the Lesson 1 questions, placing a green dot next to any question the resistivity data helped to answer (for example, 'Which materials let current flow?' and 'How can Mr Otieno hold the wire safely?'), (2) write new questions on sticky notes (for example, 'Why is copper's resistivity so much lower than glass?', 'Why does silicon conduct a little, and does temperature change it?', 'Why does the diode conduct only one way?'), and (3) cluster them under the headings Conductors and Insulators, Semiconductors, and Applications. Wanjiku and Kamau add the question: 'If all materials have electrons, why do some not let them move?' Each learner reads one question to a partner and says which later lesson might answer it.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at our DQB. Which questions can we now answer with evidence from today? Place a green dot and say the evidence.' Give 4 minutes for writing new questions and say: 'Write questions about WHY, not just WHAT.' WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds while learners think before cold-calling 3 learners to read a new question aloud. Ask: 'Which cluster does this belong to? Is it a question about the data, the cause or an application?' Group similar questions and model rewriting a vague one: 'Why is silicon special?' becomes 'Why does silicon conduct a little and more when warmer?' Link to the driving question: 'Which of these questions will help us explain the safety and efficiency of wiring, solar panels, computers and MRI machines?' Do not answer the why questions; mark them as coming next.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Question clustering on a public Driving Question Board (DQB). Tracking questions and evidence lets learners see their own progress and shows how new investigations will address unresolved questions, keeping the whole unit connected to the driving question.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that each learner has at least one new question and that at least half are 'why' or 'how' questions. Check green dots are accompanied by a stated piece of evidence (for example, 'PVC about 10^13 ohm metre'). Note whether questions mention electrons, energy or temperature, which shows readiness for the later lessons. Record which learners still ask only 'what' questions for follow-up support.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revise the class model, the cumulative drawing of electrons, atoms and energy bands begun in Lesson 1. In groups, they add: (1) a resistivity scale (a vertical or horizontal line with copper 10^-8, germanium 0.46, silicon 10^3, wood and glass 10^8 to 10^14, and PVC at 10^13 or more), (2) three labelled zones, conductor, semiconductor and insulator, with an example of each from the test circuit, (3) a sketch of Mr Otieno's cable showing a copper core with arrows for current flow and a PVC cover with a label 'almost no current escapes', and (4) a '?' sign beside the idea 'why do electrons move easily in copper but hardly at all in PVC?' to show an unfinished part of the model. Each group presents its revised model to another group, which gives one 'I like' and one 'I wonder' comment. Finally, learners complete the first two columns of the summary table (What we observed, What we learned) and start the third (What we can explain).
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Our model must now show how good or poor each material is, not just yes or no.' Provide chart paper and markers. Ask: 'What did we add from today's data? Show where the evidence is in your drawing.' Circulate with prompts: 'Where on your scale does silicon go? What does that say about how well it conducts?' and 'How does your drawing show why the PVC is safe?' WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds before asking a group to justify a change. Cold-call 3 groups to explain one revision and one remaining question. Praise any group who marks a '?' for the cause of the differences. Close: 'We can say WHAT is different: resistivity differs by more than 20 powers of ten. Next we ask WHY, starting with silicon and germanium.' Collect the summary table drafts.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision with gallery critique. Adding evidence to the class model, and marking explicitly what it cannot yet explain, helps learners see models as tools that improve with data. Peer 'I like, I wonder' feedback encourages evidence-based critique.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for models that include: a scale with correct order (copper, germanium, silicon, wood, glass, PVC); the three categories correctly assigned; a labelled cable with copper and PVC; and an honest question mark for the unexplained cause. Listen for learners using almost no current. Use a quick self-check: learners show 1-4 fingers for how confident they are in explaining why wiring uses copper with PVC. Follow up with those showing 1-2.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: 1) Did learners treat the resistivity numbers as evidence, or did they only copy them down? Which questions helped them notice the very large gaps between powers of ten? 2) How many learners still say insulators have zero conduction or use no current? Plan to revisit with 'almost no current' in the next lesson's opening. 3) Did learners separate WHAT (classification) from WHY (the energy gap explanation)? Did the open questions on the DQB point to the energy bands and semiconductors? 4) Which groups struggled with powers of ten or with the 1/rho calculation and need support? 5) Were all safety rules respected (3 V only, no short circuits, no discussion of experimenting with mains)? 6) How did Kenyan contexts such as Mr Otieno's wiring in Nairobi help learners connect to the phenomenon? What local examples (for example, a jua kali electrician or a damaged extension cable) could be added?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We re-ran the test circuit (3 V, bulb): copper bright; glass, dry wood and plastic off; silicon diode lit forward and off in reverse. The resistivity card showed copper about 1.7 x 10^-8 ohm metre, germanium 0.46, silicon 2.3 x 10^3, dry wood about 10^8 to 10^11, glass about 10^10 to 10^14 and PVC about 10^13 or more. Silicon is about 1.4 x 10^11 times more resistive than copper.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Materials can be classified by resistivity: conductors (copper) have very low resistivity; semiconductors (germanium and silicon) are in between; insulators (wood, glass, PVC) have very high resistivity and allow almost no current. Conductivity is 1/rho. Household wiring uses copper for efficient current flow and PVC to keep current inside the wire so people can handle cables safely.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: We can explain why Mr Otieno uses copper cable covered in PVC for a Nairobi house at 240 V: copper's low resistivity carries current efficiently and PVC's very high resistivity almost stops current reaching a person. We cannot yet explain WHY the resistivities differ so much or why silicon conducts a little, which we will investigate next.

LESSONS.title: Intrinsic Semiconductors: Silicon and Germanium
LESSONS.aresKeywords: intrinsic semiconductor, silicon, germanium, energy gap, band gap, free electron, hole, electron-hole pair, temperature, conductivity, resistivity

slo.purpose: Students investigate why pure (intrinsic) silicon and germanium conduct a little, and why their conductivity rises when they are warmer, using energy gaps and resistivity data to revise the class model.
slo.knowledge: Intrinsic means pure. Silicon (Eg 1.1 eV, rho about 2.3 x 10^3 ohm metre) and germanium (Eg 0.67 eV, rho about 0.46 ohm metre) have a small energy gap, so at room temperature a few electrons gain enough energy to become free electrons. Each freed electron leaves a hole, making an electron-hole pair. Higher temperature frees more pairs, so conductivity rises (resistivity falls). Copper, a metal, behaves differently: its resistance rises slightly with temperature. Germanium has the smaller gap and so is less resistive than silicon.
slo.skills: Developing and using models (NGSS SEP 2): revise the class model of electrons, atoms and energy bands to show electron-hole pairs. Analysing and interpreting data (SEP 4): compare gaps and resistivities and read a temperature trend. Constructing explanations (SEP 6): explain with evidence why silicon conducts a little and more when warm. Communication and collaboration: share ideas in pairs and with the class.
slo.attitudes: Curiosity about why the same atoms behave differently. Responsibility when handling warm water and electrical equipment. Respect for peers' ideas when revising models. Appreciation of how semiconductor science supports Kenyan technology such as phones and solar kits.
slo.keyInquiry: How do semiconductors and superconductors differ from ordinary conductors and insulators? (This lesson addresses pure semiconductors.)
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lesson 1 students saw the bulb light for copper only and the diode conduct one way, and made a first class model. Lesson 2 classified materials by resistivity into conductors, insulators and semiconductors. Lesson 3 explains why silicon and germanium sit in between, by adding an energy gap and electron-hole pairs to the class model, and shows that temperature changes conduction. This prepares Lesson 4, where students ask how doping gives control, and answers part of the DQB question about what makes the semiconductor in between so useful.
slo.safetyNotes: Use only the 3 V supply (two 1.5 V dry cells). Never use mains electricity in class. Warm water for the temperature activity must be hand-hot (no hotter than about 50 C), poured by the teacher; keep the diode and clips dry, using a sealed plastic bag if needed. Do not touch hot water containers without a cloth. Dry hands before touching circuits. Dispose of nothing electrical in water. Wash hands after the lesson.

LESSONS.overview: Ms Achieng reminds the class of Mr Otieno's copper cable in PVC in the Nairobi house, and of Lesson 2's resistivity order: copper lowest, then germanium, then silicon, then wood, then glass and PVC. Wanjiku and Kamau ask why silicon is not an insulator, since its atoms hold electrons just like glass. Students predict how a silicon semiconductor will behave when it is warmed, then observe evidence: an energy gap and resistivity data card for silicon, germanium, copper and glass, plus a demonstration using the 3 V test circuit with the 1N4007 silicon diode, forward-connected, where the bulb lit in Lesson 1, and a class analysis of a temperature trend dataset for pure silicon. Students then explain, using the energy gap idea, why a few electrons are freed and how holes appear. They add questions to the Driving Question Board (DQB) and revise the class model by adding a small gap, electron-hole pairs and the effect of temperature.

framework.learnerExperience: Students look at the Lesson 2 resistivity order on the board (copper 1.7 x 10^-8, germanium 0.46, silicon 2.3 x 10^3, dry wood 10^8 to 10^11, glass 10^10 to 10^14, PVC 10^13 or more ohm metre). Ms Achieng poses: 'Pure silicon is much more resistive than copper but far less resistive than glass. In Nairobi at midday the room is warm; at night it is cool. Predict what happens to the conduction of a pure silicon piece when it is warmed.' Each student silently writes a prediction in their notebook with a quick sketch of silicon atoms and electrons, and finishes the sentence: 'I think warming silicon will make it conduct ___ because ___.' Pairs then compare, and note whether they think copper will behave the same way.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the resistivity order. Say: 'Remember Mr Otieno's copper cable and PVC cover. Silicon sits in between. Before I give you any new information, I want your best thinking.' Give 2 minutes of silent writing, then 1 minute pair talk. WAIT TIME: after asking 'What do you think happens when silicon is warmed?', wait 10-15 seconds before taking any answer. Cold-call 4 pairs (not volunteers) and record predictions as tallies on the board: more, less, same. Ask 'What are you assuming about the electrons in silicon?' Do not say which is right. Say: 'Keep your prediction; we will test it with evidence.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain with public commitment: writing a prediction and sketching the electron picture before instruction surfaces ideas (for example that all electrons in silicon are stuck or all are free) so students can later compare them with evidence, which makes the conceptual change visible and memorable.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check notebooks for: (a) a clear prediction (more, less or same); (b) a reason that mentions electrons or energy; (c) whether students link silicon to Lesson 2's in-between resistivity. Look for the misconception that warming makes silicon behave like a metal (resistance rises) or that insulators and semiconductors are the same. Record the tally on the board and note which students gave no reasoning, for follow-up in the Explain phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Students gather evidence in three parts (about 14 minutes). Part A: Each group receives an evidence card with energy gaps at about 300 K (copper 0 eV, bands overlap; germanium 0.67 eV; silicon 1.1 eV; glass above about 5 eV) and resistivity values from Lesson 2. They rank materials by gap and by resistivity and record that the order matches: smaller gap, lower resistivity. Part B: Ms Achieng runs the Lesson 1 test circuit (3 V from two 1.5 V dry cells, 3 V torch bulb, crocodile clips) with the 1N4007 silicon diode forward-connected: the bulb lit. Then she warms the diode in a sealed bag in hand-hot water while students watch the bulb and observe a small change. Students record what they see. Part C: Groups analyse a temperature dataset for pure silicon, showing resistivity falling as temperature rises, and a copper dataset showing resistance rising slightly with temperature. They sketch two graphs of conductivity against temperature (one for silicon rising, one for copper slightly falling).
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute the evidence cards and circuit materials. Say: 'Wanjiku and Kamau are asking: what do the numbers tell us about why silicon is in between?' Circulate and ask: 'Which has the smaller gap, silicon or germanium? Which has the lower resistivity? What pattern do you see?' For Part B, demonstrate with the supply at 3 V only and remind: 'Warm water only, hand-hot, dry clips.' State the safe circuit rules. Ask: 'What do you notice about the bulb?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before taking answers. Be honest that a torch bulb is a crude detector and a small change may be hard to see; say: 'A bulb is not sensitive, so we use the dataset to see the trend clearly.' Cold-call 3 groups to describe the silicon trend and 2 groups to describe the copper trend. Do not yet explain why; say: 'Hold your explanation until the next phase.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data analysis with pattern finding: ranking gap and resistivity side by side lets students notice the relationship themselves before the idea is named, and contrasting silicon and copper graphs builds the observation that temperature has opposite effects on semiconductors and metals.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe whether groups: (1) rank materials correctly (copper, germanium, silicon, glass) by both gap and resistivity; (2) state that silicon's conductivity rises with temperature using data (for example 'resistivity went down as temperature went up'); (3) correctly say copper's resistance rises slightly. Listen for confusion between resistivity and conductivity and prompt: 'Conductivity is the reverse of resistivity (1/rho).' Note any group that reports the bulb as a precise measurement.

framework.learnerExperience: Students use the energy band picture to explain their observations. Ms Achieng draws two bands: a full valence band and an empty conduction band separated by a gap. Pairs explain: (1) why copper, with no gap (0 eV), conducts easily, (2) why glass, with a gap above about 5 eV, has almost no free electrons, and (3) why silicon (1.1 eV) and germanium (0.67 eV) have a few. Students learn that at room temperature a few electrons gain enough thermal energy to jump the gap and become free electrons, and each leaves behind a hole, forming an electron-hole pair; both can carry current. Warming gives more electrons enough energy, so more pairs form and conductivity rises. Because germanium's gap is smaller, more electrons cross at the same temperature, so germanium has lower resistivity than silicon. Students write a 3-sentence explanation using the words energy gap, free electron, hole, temperature and compare with their earlier prediction. They also explain that copper's resistance rises slightly with temperature but this is a different effect from the semiconductor trend, and note that pure silicon is still electrically neutral.
framework.teacherMoves: Draw the band diagram and say: 'Here is the gap. Where is silicon on this picture? Where is copper? Where is glass?' Use a think-pair-share: 1 minute of pair talk, then cold-call 4 pairs to explain one part each. WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before each cold call. Probe with: 'Why does a free electron leave a hole behind?', 'Is the silicon charged after electrons are freed?' (answer: no, still neutral overall), and 'Why would germanium conduct more than silicon at the same temperature?' Use the phrase 'almost no' when discussing glass: say 'Glass conducts almost none, not zero.' Do not call semiconductors half conductors. Do not teach doping; if a student asks how to make silicon conduct better, say: 'Great question, put it on the DQB; Lesson 4 will investigate it.' Ask students to compare to their prediction and use the sentence frame: 'My prediction was ___ and the evidence shows ___ because ___.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning with a band diagram: students make a claim about temperature and conduction, support it with data from the evidence card and dataset, and reason with the energy gap model, which connects the observations to a particle-level mechanism and links to the Nairobi wiring phenomenon.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check written explanations for: (a) a correct statement that a small gap lets a few electrons become free; (b) mention of both free electrons and holes as pairs; (c) correct link between higher temperature and more pairs and higher conductivity; (d) correct comparison of germanium and silicon by gap. Look for errors such as 'holes are positive particles that are added' or 'warming adds electrons to silicon'. Use a quick whiteboard check: 'Which gap is smaller, silicon or germanium, and which conducts more?' Expect at least most students to answer correctly; reteach with the band diagram for those who do not.

framework.learnerExperience: Students revisit the Class DQB. Using sticky notes, each pair writes one question that this lesson answered and one new question it raised. Possible examples: 'How can we make silicon conduct much more?', 'Why does the diode conduct only one way?', 'Why do solar panels use silicon?', 'Do superconductors have a gap?', 'Does warming help or harm computers?' Pairs place notes under headings 'Answered so far', 'Partly answered' and 'Still to investigate'. They link the answered note about why silicon conducts a little to the original puzzle: why metals like copper carry current easily while plastic and wood do not, and what makes the semiconductor in between so useful.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Wanjiku and Kamau keep the DQB. What can we now answer, and what do we still need to find out?' Give 3 minutes for writing. WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after asking 'Which question is still puzzling you most?' Cold-call 3 pairs to read and place a note. Group similar questions and point out the doping and diode questions: 'These will be the focus of Lesson 4.' Move the question 'Why do some materials conduct a little?' to 'Partly answered' and ask students to justify it with evidence from today. Make sure at least one note asks about practical uses such as phones, M-Pesa or solar kits.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Question tracking on a shared board: sorting questions by how far they are answered makes progress visible, links each lesson to the driving question and motivates the next investigation by turning curiosity into a coherent path.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that notes are specific (for example 'Why does doping increase conductivity?' rather than 'What is a semiconductor?'), that pairs sort at least one note correctly, and that new questions build on today's idea of electron-hole pairs and temperature. Count how many pairs wrote a question linked to a Kenyan application. Note students who only restate facts rather than ask a question.

framework.learnerExperience: Students revise the class model of electrons, atoms and energy bands made in Lesson 1. Using coloured markers, each group adds to the class model: (1) a small energy gap for silicon (1.1 eV) and germanium (0.67 eV) compared with copper (0 eV) and glass (above about 5 eV); (2) a few electrons jumping the gap to become free electrons at room temperature; (3) a hole left behind in the valence band, shown as an electron-hole pair; (4) more pairs when temperature increases, with an arrow labelled 'warmer, more pairs, higher conductivity'; and (5) a note that copper's resistance rises slightly with temperature. Groups write a short caption linking the model to the Nairobi house: 'Copper carries current and PVC insulates; silicon is in between and controlled by temperature.' They also record a model limitation: pure silicon conducts too little to be very useful, so what could change that?
framework.teacherMoves: Display the class model and say: 'Our model started in Lesson 1 with just electrons and atoms. What must we add today so that it explains silicon?' Give 8 minutes for groups to revise. Circulate with: 'Where in your model is the hole? What makes more pairs?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after asking 'What is still missing from our model?' Cold-call 3 groups to explain one change each, and invite another group to challenge with evidence. Confirm that the model correctly shows neutral silicon and the same fixed numbers (1.1 eV, 0.67 eV). End by saying: 'Pure silicon conducts a little and more when warmer. In Lesson 4 we ask how we can control it.' Collect the group captions.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision: adding new elements to a shared model and stating limitations shows students how scientific explanations improve as evidence accumulates, and gives a visible representation they can reuse to explain the phenomenon in later lessons.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for models that show: a gap smaller than the insulator gap and larger than zero; electrons and holes created together; more pairs at higher temperature; copper treated differently. Check captions use the conventions (conductor, insulator, semiconductor, intrinsic, free electrons, holes). Use an exit prompt: 'In one sentence, why does warming increase the conduction of pure silicon?' Success looks like 'warming gives more electrons enough energy to cross the gap, forming more electron-hole pairs.'

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, consider: Did students use the energy gap rather than just stating that warming makes silicon conduct more? Which students held the idea that holes are real particles added to silicon or that silicon becomes charged, and how did the band diagram change their thinking? Was the bulb change too small to see, and did students correctly rely on the dataset instead? Did students keep intrinsic silicon distinct from doped silicon, leaving doping for Lesson 4? Which DQB questions show readiness for doping and diodes? How well did cold-calling and 10-15 seconds of wait time bring in quieter students? What would you change in the safety routine with warm water?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed that the silicon diode (1N4007) forward-connected lit the 3 V bulb, as in Lesson 1, and that the data show silicon (rho about 2.3 x 10^3 ohm metre) and germanium (about 0.46 ohm metre) are far more resistive than copper (1.7 x 10^-8 ohm metre) but far less than glass. The temperature dataset showed the resistivity of pure silicon falling as it was warmed, while copper's resistance rose slightly.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned that pure (intrinsic) silicon and germanium have a small energy gap (1.1 eV and 0.67 eV), so at room temperature a few electrons gain enough energy to become free electrons, each leaving a hole to make an electron-hole pair. Germanium, with the smaller gap, conducts more than silicon. Warming creates more pairs so conductivity rises.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: We explained that silicon conducts a little because its small gap lets a few electrons cross, unlike glass, wood and PVC with a gap above about 5 eV that allow almost no free electrons, and unlike copper, where the bands overlap. This helps explain why semiconductors sit between copper wire and its plastic cover in Mr Otieno's Nairobi house, and raises the question of how to control their conduction, which we will investigate next.

LESSONS.title: Doping: Making n-type and p-type Semiconductors
LESSONS.duration: 40 minutes (double period of 80 minutes recommended if the model-building phase is extended)
LESSONS.aresKeywords: doping, extrinsic semiconductor, intrinsic semiconductor, n-type, p-type, phosphorus, boron, free electrons, holes, majority carriers, p-n junction, diode, forward-biased, reverse-biased

slo.purpose: Students explain how doping pure silicon with phosphorus or boron makes extrinsic n-type or p-type semiconductors, and why this control makes semiconductors useful, including how a p-n junction gives the diode its one-way action in the bulb test.
slo.knowledge: Doping adds a very small number of impurity atoms (about 1 atom in 10^7 to 10^8) to pure (intrinsic) silicon. Phosphorus (group 5, 5 valence electrons) gives one extra free electron per atom, making n-type silicon with electrons as majority carriers. Boron (group 3, 3 valence electrons) leaves one missing electron, a hole, per atom, making p-type silicon with holes as majority carriers. Doped silicon is still electrically neutral overall. Doping raises conductivity by a factor of many thousands in a controlled way. Joining p-type and n-type gives a p-n junction, a diode that conducts when forward-biased (bulb lit) and not when reverse-biased (bulb off).
slo.skills: Developing and using models (drawing atom-level pictures of n-type and p-type silicon); analysing and interpreting data (comparing conductivity of pure and doped silicon); constructing explanations (why the diode conducted one way only); communication and collaboration in pairs and groups.
slo.attitudes: Curiosity about how tiny changes in a material produce big changes in behaviour; responsibility when handling circuit components and sharing roles; respect for others' ideas when peer-reviewing models; appreciation of how electronics shapes daily life in Kenya (phones, M-Pesa, solar kits).
slo.keyInquiry: How do semiconductors and superconductors differ from ordinary conductors and insulators? How is electronics applied in day-to-day life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 3 showed that pure silicon and germanium have a small energy gap (1.1 eV and 0.67 eV), so only a few electron and hole pairs form and conductivity rises with temperature. Students now ask: if pure silicon conducts so poorly (resistivity 2.3 x 10^3 ohm metre against 1.7 x 10^-8 for copper), how can it be useful? Doping gives the answer and explains the diode in the Lesson 1 test: why the bulb lit in one direction only. This prepares Lesson 5 (testing the band model with a simulation) and Lesson 7 (solar panels and microchips).
slo.safetyNotes: Use only the low-voltage 3 V circuit (two 1.5 V dry cells) with the 1N4007 diode; never connect the diode or any component to mains 240 V. Check that clips do not short-circuit the cells (cells and wires may get warm). Do not touch exposed wire ends of damaged cable. Dispose of used cells at a collection point, not in the open. No chemicals are handled; doping is modelled with counters and drawings only.

LESSONS.overview: Ms Achieng opens by returning to the diode result from the five-material test: the bulb lit when the 1N4007 was forward-connected and stayed off when reverse-connected. Students first predict how a tiny amount of another element might change pure silicon. They then re-run the diode test in both directions to recollect the evidence, and use a counter-based bead model (a grid of silicon atoms with phosphorus or boron substitutions) to see where extra free electrons and holes come from. In the Explain phase they use the doping ratio (1 atom in 10^7 to 10^8) and the claim that conductivity rises many thousands of times to argue why doping is useful, and they connect a p-n junction to the one-way action of the diode. Students add new questions to the Driving Question Board (DQB) and revise the class model to include n-type and p-type regions. Throughout, the Nairobi electrician Mr Otieno's copper cable and the silicon chips in phones and the Garissa solar plant anchor the ideas.

framework.learnerExperience: Students recall the Lesson 1 test: copper lit the bulb; glass, dry wood and plastic did not; the silicon diode lit the bulb forward-connected and not reverse-connected. On a prediction sheet they individually answer: 'Pure silicon has resistivity about 2.3 x 10^3 ohm metre, about 10^11 times more resistive than copper. If we replace just 1 silicon atom in every 10 million to 100 million with phosphorus or boron, what will happen to its conductivity? Sketch what you think the atoms and electrons look like.' They commit to one of three options: (a) no change, (b) small change, (c) very large change, and give a reason. They share with a partner, then a few share with the class.
framework.teacherMoves: Hold up the 1N4007 diode and say: "Remember Wanjiku and Kamau's test: the bulb lit one way and not the other. Today we find out why. Silicon is the main material inside this diode." Write the three options on the board. Say: "Take 2 minutes to write your prediction and draw it. There are no wrong predictions today, only ideas to test." Circulate and note common ideas (for example 'adding anything makes it worse' or 'impurities do nothing'). Then ask: "Turn to your partner and explain your reason in 30 seconds." Cold-call 4 pairs, giving WAIT TIME of 10 to 15 seconds after each question: "Why did you choose that option?" Do not say which is correct. Record the vote count (a/b/c) on the board.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (POE) with a public vote: committing to a prediction makes learners' existing ideas visible, so that later evidence creates a genuine need to revise them. Sketching atoms and electrons (developing models) links the prediction to the class model begun in Lesson 1.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check prediction sheets for: (1) a clear choice of a, b or c; (2) a reason that mentions electrons or atoms rather than only 'it is silicon'; (3) a sketch that shows electrons, atoms or gaps. Tally how many learners chose (c) very large change. Note learners who say impurities must reduce conductivity, who will need the evidence in the next phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Part A (10 minutes): In groups of 4 using the standard circuit (3 V from two 1.5 V dry cells in series, 3 V torch bulb, crocodile clips), students re-test the 1N4007 diode forward-connected (bulb lit) and reverse-connected (bulb off), recording in a table with bulb brightness and the direction of the diode's marked band relative to the cell. Part B (10 minutes): Students use a model grid of 25 'silicon atoms' (grey counters, each with 4 outer electrons shown as dots) and then (i) replace 1 counter with a 'phosphorus' counter (5 dots) and note the extra electron; (ii) replace another grid with a 'boron' counter (3 dots) and note the missing electron (a hole shown as an empty circle). They also read a short data card: 'Pure silicon: 2.3 x 10^3 ohm metre. Doping about 1 atom in 10^7 to 10^8 with phosphorus or boron raises conductivity by a factor of many thousands.' They record observations: what moved, what stayed, and where the electron or hole is.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute materials and say: "Roles: circuit builder, recorder, timekeeper, materials manager. Swap roles for Part B." Remind: "Only the 3 V cells. No mains. If a clip or cell feels warm, disconnect and call me." For Part A ask: "Which direction lit the bulb? How do you know the diode is reversed?" For Part B model the first substitution at one group's table: "Silicon has 4 outer electrons and shares them with 4 neighbours. Phosphorus has 5. How many are left over after bonding?" WAIT TIME of 10 to 15 seconds. Then: "Boron has 3. How many bonds can it complete, and what is missing?" Cold-call 3 groups to describe one observation each. Prompt: "Is the doped silicon charged overall? Count the protons and electrons." Listen for the idea that each added atom is neutral, so the doped silicon is still electrically neutral overall. Circulate with an observation checklist.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Evidence gathering with a physical model (counter-based analogy) and a structured data table: learners see from the model where the free electron or hole comes from, while the data card gives the scale (1 in 10^7 to 10^8) and effect (thousands of times more conductive). Linking the concrete circuit result to the atom-level model supports claim-evidence-reasoning later.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: groups correctly record forward (lit) and reverse (off); counters show 1 extra dot for phosphorus and 1 empty circle (hole) for boron; learners say 'free electron' for n-type and 'hole' for p-type (conventions); they state that doped silicon stays neutral. Use a checklist to note groups that call a hole a 'positive particle added' rather than a missing electron, and address it in the Explain phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Students work in their groups to write a claim-evidence-reasoning (CER) explanation answering: 'Why is doped silicon more useful in electronics than pure silicon, and why did the diode light the bulb in only one direction?' They must use: phosphorus and n-type (extra free electrons, electrons as majority carriers); boron and p-type (holes as majority carriers); the doping ratio (1 in 10^7 to 10^8) and the effect (conductivity thousands of times higher, controlled by how much dopant is added); and the p-n junction (a p-type piece joined to an n-type piece) as the structure of the diode. They draw a labelled picture of a p-n junction and use arrows to show that the bulb lights forward-biased and not reverse-biased. They then compare their explanation with another group using a feedback checklist and revise one sentence. Finally they re-open their Predict sheet and write, 'My prediction was ... The evidence shows ... So I now think ...'.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Use the evidence from the bulb and the counters, not just what you remember. Your claim must answer the question in one sentence." Give sentence frames on the board: 'Doping with phosphorus gives ___ so the majority carriers are ___.' 'Doping with boron gives ___ so the majority carriers are ___.' Ask the class: "Pure silicon is about 10^11 times more resistive than copper. Why can we not just use copper in a diode?" WAIT TIME of 10 to 15 seconds, then cold-call 3 learners. Address the misconception directly: "A hole is not a new particle added. It is a missing electron. And doped silicon is still neutral." Then say: "Why is controlling the amount of dopant powerful? Think about a phone chip in Nairobi with billions of transistors." Cold-call 3 more learners. For the junction, say: "When the diode is forward-biased the bulb lit, when reverse-biased it was off. What does the junction let through, and what does it hold back?" Accept answers that carriers can cross in one direction only; do not go beyond the level of this lesson (details of the depletion region are not needed). Connect back: "Copper cable carries Mr Otieno's current in both directions; a diode lets it pass one way only. That is what makes it useful in solar panels and chips."
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) with peer critique: CER pushes learners to tie the claim to specific evidence (bulb results, counters, data card) and to scientific reasoning (carriers and structure). Peer feedback and the prediction revision make the change in thinking explicit, which strengthens conceptual change.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for explanations that: (1) correctly name phosphorus as n-type with extra free electrons and boron as p-type with holes; (2) state the majority carriers; (3) cite 1 in 10^7 to 10^8 and a large rise in conductivity; (4) state that doped silicon is still neutral; (5) link the p-n junction to forward (lit) and reverse (off) results. Mark each group against these five points. Learners who describe a hole as a positive atom or say doping makes silicon a conductor like copper need a short follow-up conversation. Ask 3 learners to give an exit-ticket sentence on why the diode works one way.

framework.learnerExperience: Students return to the Class DQB, which holds questions from earlier lessons. In pairs, they (1) put a tick on questions now partly or fully answered by today's evidence (for example 'Why does the diode work in one direction only?' and 'Why is silicon useful?'), writing a short evidence note on a sticky note; and (2) add at least one new question arising from this lesson, such as 'How does a p-n junction make electricity in a solar panel at Garissa?', 'How much dopant is needed?', 'Can we dope germanium too?' or 'What happens when a diode is heated?'. They sort new questions into categories: Doping, Diodes and junctions, Solar and microchips, Superconductors and MRI.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Go to the DQB with your partner. Find one question that today's work helps answer and one new question you now have." Allow 5 minutes. Then ask: "Which question did we answer, and what is your evidence?" WAIT TIME of 10 to 15 seconds. Cold-call 3 pairs. Say: "Which new question will Lesson 5 (the simulation) help with? Which one must wait for Lessons 6 and 7?" Cold-call 2 pairs. Point out the link: "Several of you asked about solar panels. Garissa solar plant is about 50 MW and uses silicon p-n junctions. We will return to it in Lesson 7." Move any question that was answered to the 'Answered' column with the evidence note attached.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board as a public record of growing understanding: connecting new questions to evidence maintains learner ownership of the unit and shows which ideas still need investigation, which motivates the following lessons.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe whether sticky notes give evidence (for example 'bulb lit forward only') rather than just 'we learned it'. Check that new questions are specific to doping or junctions and not repeats of old ones. Count how many pairs add a question that links to Kenyan applications (solar kits, M-Pesa phones, Garissa plant), which shows transfer.

framework.learnerExperience: Students revise the cumulative class model (the drawing of electrons, atoms and energy bands). Each group adds to the Lesson 3 model: (1) a panel for n-type silicon showing a phosphorus atom, one extra free electron, and the label 'majority carriers: electrons'; (2) a panel for p-type silicon showing a boron atom, a hole, and 'majority carriers: holes'; (3) a p-n junction drawn as p-type joined to n-type, with the diode symbol, and an arrow with 'forward-biased: bulb lit' and 'reverse-biased: bulb off'. They label where the doping ratio applies (about 1 in 10^7 to 10^8) and note that both pieces remain neutral overall. Groups then do a gallery walk, leaving one star (something clear) and one wish (something to improve) on each model.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Take the Lesson 3 class model. We are not starting again; we are adding to it. What must we add to explain the diode and why doping is useful?" Give 8 minutes for revision. Circulate and ask: "Where is the free electron in your n-type drawing? Where is the hole in the p-type? Is your doped silicon charged?"
