WAIT TIME of 10 to 15 seconds for each. Then say: "Gallery walk: visit two other groups. Leave one star and one wish." Cold-call 3 groups to share what they changed from their previous model and why, referencing evidence. Pin the best consensus version as the Class model for the board. Close by asking: "Our model now explains the diode. What does it not yet explain? How does it connect to energy bands?" Take 2 responses and note that Lesson 5 will test the band model with a simulation.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision with peer gallery walk: revising the same model each lesson shows how scientific ideas grow with evidence. Star-and-wish feedback encourages learners to evaluate models against evidence and to identify gaps that lead to the next investigation.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check each model for: n-type with phosphorus, extra free electron and electrons as majority carriers; p-type with boron, hole and holes as majority carriers; a p-n junction labelled with forward (lit) and reverse (off); neutrality stated; correct conventions (intrinsic, extrinsic, forward-biased, reverse-biased). Record which groups can say what the model cannot yet explain. Use a 3-point rubric: complete, mostly complete, needs support.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, ask yourself: Did learners distinguish a hole as a missing electron rather than a particle, and did they keep in mind that doped silicon is still neutral? Which prediction option (a, b or c) did most learners choose at the start, and how did it change by the end? Did every group link the bulb result (forward lit, reverse off) to a p-n junction? Were the cold-call and WAIT TIME routines used so that quieter learners such as those who rarely speak were heard? What new DQB questions suggest that learners need more time before the Lesson 5 simulation? Note any learners who need support with the idea of majority carriers and plan a short revisit using the counters.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We re-tested the 1N4007 diode: the bulb lit when it was forward-connected (forward-biased) and stayed off when it was reverse-connected (reverse-biased). Using counters, we saw that replacing one silicon atom with phosphorus (5 outer electrons) leaves an extra free electron, and replacing one with boron (3 outer electrons) leaves a hole. The data card showed that doping about 1 atom in 10^7 to 10^8 raises the conductivity of silicon by a factor of many thousands.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Doping makes extrinsic semiconductors from pure (intrinsic) silicon. Phosphorus gives n-type (majority carriers: electrons) and boron gives p-type (majority carriers: holes). Doped silicon is still electrically neutral overall. Doping lets us control conductivity, and joining p-type and n-type makes a p-n junction, which is the diode.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Pure silicon conducts very poorly (resistivity about 2.3 x 10^3 ohm metre), but a tiny amount of phosphorus or boron adds free electrons or holes, so conductivity rises thousands of times in a controlled way. A p-n junction lets current pass when forward-biased (bulb lit) and blocks it when reverse-biased (bulb off), which is why doped silicon is the basis of diodes, solar panels like those at Garissa, and microchips in phones and computers.

LESSONS.title: PhET Simulation: Testing the Band Model with Digital Evidence
LESSONS.duration: 40 minutes (one lesson; double period of 80 minutes if only one computer or tablet is available per group of 4)
LESSONS.aresKeywords: energy band, energy gap (band gap), conductor, insulator, semiconductor, intrinsic, extrinsic, n-type, p-type, doping, free electrons, holes, simulation, model testing, digital evidence

slo.purpose: Learners use a simulation as digital evidence to test and refine the class band model by changing the energy gap, the doping type and the temperature, and then use the evidence to explain why copper lights the bulb while glass, wood and plastic do not and why silicon sits in between. This lesson teaches the skill of testing a model, not a new concept.
slo.knowledge: Learners use the simulation to check ideas from Lessons 2 to 4: metals have an energy gap of 0 eV (bands overlap); silicon has 1.1 eV; germanium has 0.67 eV; insulators such as glass have a gap above about 5 eV, so almost no electrons can move. Raising the temperature frees more electrons in a semiconductor. Doping with phosphorus gives n-type (extra free electrons) and doping with boron gives p-type (holes), and doped silicon stays electrically neutral overall.
slo.skills: Developing and using models (NGSS SEP 2): compare model predictions with simulation output and revise the model. Planning and carrying out investigations (SEP 3): change one variable at a time (gap, temperature or doping type). Analysing and interpreting data (SEP 4): record and compare simulation readings in a table. Engaging in argument from evidence (SEP 7): judge how far a simulation can be trusted compared with the real bulb test. Digital literacy: use a simulation on a computer or tablet, working offline from the pre-loaded copy.
slo.attitudes: Curiosity and open-mindedness: willingness to revise a model when evidence disagrees. Responsibility: each group member takes a role (operator, recorder, reporter, checker). Respect and collaboration: listening to group members' predictions and giving reasons. Honesty: reporting results exactly as observed, even when they differ from the prediction.
slo.keyInquiry: 1. How do semiconductors and superconductors differ from ordinary conductors and insulators? 2. How is electronics applied in day-to-day life? (This lesson focuses on question 1 for conductors, insulators and semiconductors, and uses digital evidence to test the band model that explains the Nairobi wiring phenomenon.)
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 2 to 4 gave the class classification by resistivity, intrinsic conduction and doping. In Lesson 5 the class stops adding ideas and instead tests the band model, because real atoms and bands cannot be seen. The simulation lets learners change the gap, temperature and doping in seconds. The tested model then carries into Lesson 6 (superconductors and MRI magnets) and Lesson 7 (final model-based answer on solar panels, microchips and MRI).
slo.safetyNotes: No hazardous materials. Seat learners so that cables from tablets or laptops are not across walkways. Keep drinks away from devices. Limit screen time to about 20 minutes and let learners look away from the screen between tasks. If devices are charged from the mains, only the teacher connects and disconnects chargers. If there are fewer devices, use groups of 4 to 5, or the teacher projects the simulation and learners take turns to operate it.

LESSONS.overview: Ms Achieng reminds the class of the Nairobi house where Mr Otieno holds a PVC-covered copper cable safely while it carries current, and of the five-material bulb test (copper bright; glass, dry wood and plastic off; the silicon 1N4007 diode lit forward-biased and off reverse-biased). Learners first predict, in writing, what a band diagram will look like for a metal, silicon, germanium and an insulator, and what will happen when temperature rises or phosphorus or boron is added. Groups then use the PhET simulation as digital evidence: they change one variable at a time, record what they see in a table, and compare it with the class model and their predictions. In the Explain phase they decide which parts of the class model are supported and which need revision, and discuss the limits of a simulation compared with the real bulb test. They add new questions and partial answers to the Driving Question Board (DQB), and finally revise the class model on a poster so that it shows bands, gap sizes, free electrons, holes and temperature effects.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners look at the one-page class model from Lesson 4 and a blank set of four energy band boxes labelled copper, silicon, germanium and glass. Working alone for 3 minutes, each learner sketches what they expect: where the gap is, and how many electrons are in the upper band for each material at room temperature. They also write one-sentence predictions: (a) 'If I raise the temperature of silicon, the number of free electrons will ...' (b) 'If I add phosphorus, the extra electrons will be ...' (c) 'If I add boron, the holes will be ...' (d) 'If I make the gap bigger, such as for glass, the current will ...'. They then share predictions with a partner and star the one they are least sure about.
framework.teacherMoves: Hold up a 3 V torch bulb and the copper wire and say: "Remember Mr Otieno in Nairobi. He holds the PVC-covered copper cable while it carries current. Today we cannot see the inside of copper or glass, so we will test our band model with a simulation. First, what do YOU think it will show?" Ask learners to sketch silently. Give 3 minutes of silent writing. Say: "Do not look at your notes from Lesson 4 yet; I want your best thinking." Circulate and note common ideas. After partner talk, WAIT TIME: ask "Who can predict what happens to silicon when it gets warmer?" and wait 10 to 15 seconds before taking answers. Cold-call 4 learners from different groups and ask each "What made you think that?" Record 3 predictions on the board under the heading 'Predictions to test'. Do not say which is correct.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (POE) with elicited prior ideas: writing predictions before using the simulation makes learners commit to ideas, so any mismatch with the digital evidence becomes a reason to revise the model rather than a surprise to ignore.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check sketches for: (1) copper drawn with no gap or overlapping bands (0 eV); (2) silicon and germanium drawn with a small gap and silicon larger than germanium (1.1 eV and 0.67 eV); (3) glass drawn with a much larger gap (above about 5 eV). Tally how many learners predict that raising temperature increases free electrons in silicon. Note learners who say that insulators have 'no' conduction at all, and prompt them later to say 'almost none'. Note learners who think doped silicon becomes charged; this idea will be tested in the simulation.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of 4 (operator, recorder, reporter, checker), learners open the pre-loaded PhET simulation on conductivity and energy bands (offline copy) and run three short investigations. Investigation 1 (gap): select or set the gap for a metal (0 eV), germanium (0.67 eV), silicon (1.1 eV) and an insulator (above about 5 eV), keeping temperature the same, and record in a table how many electrons appear in the upper band and whether the simulated bulb or current reading is high, low or almost none. Investigation 2 (temperature): choose silicon and raise the temperature in 3 steps, recording the number of free electrons and holes at each step; then choose a metal if the simulation allows and note what happens. Investigation 3 (doping): add phosphorus (n-type) and then boron (p-type) to silicon, and record the majority carriers (electrons or holes), the current reading and whether the material is still neutral overall. Each group fills in a 3-column table and draws one labelled band diagram for each doped case. The checker confirms that only one variable was changed at a time.
framework.teacherMoves: Before groups start, model the first step: "Watch me. I change ONE thing only, the gap. Everything else stays the same. Why do I do that?" Cold-call 2 learners. Distribute roles with cards. Say: "Operator, click. Recorder, write exactly what you see, not what you expected. Checker, say 'one variable' if the operator changes more than one. Reporter, be ready to share." Circulate and ask each group at least one probing question: "Where is the gap for copper in your picture? What does that mean for Mr Otieno's cable?" and "What is different between silicon at the first and the third temperature step?" Use WAIT TIME of 10 to 15 seconds after each question before prompting. At the 10-minute mark call: "Stop. Look away from the screen. Stretch your neck for 20 seconds." For groups that finish early, ask them to find the gap size at which the simulated current becomes almost none and to record that value. If devices are limited, project the simulation and let each group send an operator to change the setting while the others predict aloud first.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Controlled-variable investigation with a data table: changing one variable at a time (gap, temperature, doping) lets learners link each change to one effect, which makes the simulation function as evidence rather than animation. Comparing results with their predictions builds model-testing skill (SEP 2 and SEP 3).
framework.formativeAssessment: Check tables for: metal 0 eV with high current; germanium 0.67 eV with more free electrons than silicon at the same temperature; silicon 1.1 eV with a few free electrons; insulator above about 5 eV with almost none; free electrons and holes in silicon increase as temperature rises; phosphorus gives extra free electrons (n-type, majority carriers electrons); boron gives holes (p-type, majority carriers holes). Indicators of skill: the group changes one variable at a time (checker calls it out), recorders write observed values rather than expected ones, and reporters use the terms 'free electrons', 'holes', 'energy gap'. Note groups that mix up n-type and p-type and ask them to point to the phosphorus (5 valence electrons) and boron (3 valence electrons) in the diagram.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups compare their prediction sketch with the simulation evidence and mark each prediction as 'supported', 'not supported' or 'needs more detail'. They then complete the claim-evidence-reasoning (CER) frame: Claim: 'Copper lit the bulb in Mr Otieno's test circuit while glass, wood and plastic did not because ...'; Evidence: simulation readings for gap 0 eV versus above about 5 eV; Reasoning: how the size of the energy gap controls how many electrons can move. They extend the CER to the diode: 'The silicon diode conducts only when forward-biased because ...' using the doping evidence (n-type and p-type) and what they know from Lesson 4 about the p-n junction giving one-way action. Finally, in a whole-class discussion they list two things the simulation shows well and two limits (for example it does not show real atoms, the numbers are simplified, and it cannot show the bulb or the 3 V dry cells). They decide which parts of the class model to keep, change or add.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Look at your prediction and your table. Mark each prediction: supported, not supported, or needs more detail." Give 3 minutes. Then ask: "Whose prediction was NOT supported? That is the most useful result today." Cold-call 3 groups. Model the CER sentence frame on the board and give 5 minutes for groups to write. Ask: "Mr Otieno holds the PVC cable safely. Use your evidence to explain why. Use the words energy gap and almost none." WAIT TIME of 10 to 15 seconds before taking responses. Cold-call 4 learners, asking another learner to restate each answer in their own words. Challenge misconceptions with: "If insulators have a huge gap, do they have zero conduction? What does your simulation say?" (Guide to 'almost none'.) Ask: "If we add phosphorus to silicon, is the silicon now negatively charged? Use evidence." (Guide to: still electrically neutral overall, since each phosphorus atom is also neutral.) Then ask: "A simulation is not the real world. Name one thing it did not show that the bulb test did." Take 3 answers. Record the agreed limits on the board. Do NOT re-teach doping or intrinsic conduction; only point back to the earlier lessons if a group is stuck.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) combined with model evaluation: learners must connect each claim about the Nairobi wiring phenomenon to specific simulation data and to the band model, which builds argument from evidence (SEP 7). Discussing the limits of the simulation develops the habit of judging how far any model or digital evidence can be trusted.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for CER answers that: (1) claim that copper conducts and plastic does not; (2) cite evidence such as 0 eV versus above about 5 eV; (3) reason that when the gap is large almost no electrons can move so PVC is a safe cover. Strong responses state that silicon (1.1 eV) and germanium (0.67 eV) conduct a little, more when warmer, and that phosphorus (n-type) and boron (p-type) raise conductivity in a controlled way. Check learners avoid 'zero conduction' for insulators and 'charged' for doped silicon. Ask 3 learners to give a thumbs-up, sideways or down for 'I can use the simulation to test a model' and note any thumbs-down for follow-up in Lesson 6.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revisit the class DQB with the driving question: 'Why do some materials conduct electricity while others do not, and how does this affect the safety and efficiency of household wiring and of devices such as solar panels, computers and MRI machines?' In groups they move sticky notes: they place questions that the simulation helped to answer (for example, 'Why does silicon conduct more when warm?' and 'What is the difference between n-type and p-type?') under 'Partly answered', and write the evidence on a new note, such as 'PhET: silicon free electrons rose at three higher temperatures'. They also write at least one new question the simulation raised, such as 'How does a p-n junction make a solar panel produce electricity?', 'What happens to resistance at very low temperatures?' or 'How can an MRI magnet carry large current without losing energy?', and add it to the DQB.
framework.teacherMoves: Point to the DQB and say: "Let us check our board. Which of our questions did today's evidence help answer, even a little?" WAIT TIME of 10 to 15 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners to move a question and justify it with one piece of evidence from their table. Say: "A good note names the evidence, for example 'In the simulation, silicon at the highest temperature had more free electrons.'" Ask each group to write one NEW question and read it aloud; say: "Which of these questions will Lesson 6 and Lesson 7 help us answer?" Flag the questions about low temperature and MRI magnets for Lesson 6, and solar panels, microchips and the Garissa solar plant (50 MW) for Lesson 7. Do not answer them yet; say: "Keep them on the board. We will come back with evidence."
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board as a living record: moving questions between 'unanswered', 'partly answered' and 'answered', and attaching evidence to each move, makes the growth in understanding visible and gives learners ownership of the next steps in the investigation.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that notes moved to 'Partly answered' name specific simulation evidence (not just 'because the teacher said so'). Count the new questions: aim for at least one per group, with at least one linked to superconductors or MRI (Lesson 6) and one to solar panels or microchips (Lesson 7). Note any group whose new question repeats an earlier one and prompt them to sharpen it with 'How' or 'Why' and a Kenyan context, for example Kenyatta National Hospital or the Garissa solar plant.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the cumulative class model (the drawing of electrons, atoms and energy bands) started in Lesson 1 and revised in Lessons 2 to 4. In their groups they add and revise: (1) four band diagrams side by side for copper (0 eV, bands overlap), germanium (0.67 eV), silicon (1.1 eV) and glass/PVC (above about 5 eV); (2) arrows or dots showing more free electrons and holes in silicon at higher temperature; (3) n-type silicon with phosphorus (extra free electrons) and p-type silicon with boron (holes), with a note that doped silicon is still electrically neutral overall; (4) a short caption connecting each diagram to the bulb test (copper bright, glass, wood and plastic off, diode lit forward-biased and off reverse-biased). Each group marks with a coloured pen one change they made to the model because of the simulation evidence. Groups then do a 'gallery walk', placing a tick or a question mark on another group's model. Each learner completes the summary table.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Look at our class model. Does it explain why Mr Otieno can safely hold the PVC-covered copper cable? What must we ADD or CHANGE after today's evidence?" Give 8 minutes for group drawing. Say: "Use a colour pen for every change you make because of evidence. Write the reason next to it." Circulate and ask: "Where in your model can I see the energy gap? Where are the free electrons? Where are the holes?" WAIT TIME of 10 to 15 seconds. For the gallery walk (4 minutes), say: "Leave one tick for something clear and one question mark for something unclear." Cold-call 3 groups to explain one change and the evidence for it. Close by saying: "Our model now has digital evidence behind it. In Lesson 6 we will test it on a new question: what happens to resistance when a material is cooled below a critical temperature, and how does that help an MRI machine?" Collect the summary tables.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision with evidence-tagged changes: colour-coding each revision to a piece of evidence trains learners to justify changes to a model, while the gallery walk provides peer critique. This keeps the model tied to the Nairobi wiring phenomenon and prepares it for the superconductor and MRI evidence.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check each group model for: copper with overlapping bands (0 eV); germanium (0.67 eV) with a smaller gap than silicon (1.1 eV); glass/PVC with a gap above about 5 eV; free electrons and holes increasing with temperature in silicon; n-type (phosphorus, majority carriers electrons) and p-type (boron, majority carriers holes) shown clearly with a note on overall neutrality; captions linking to the bulb test. Indicator of progress: at least one coloured change per group with a written reason that cites simulation evidence. Use the gallery walk question marks to identify the most common unclear ideas to address at the start of Lesson 6.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, consider: (1) Did every learner change only one variable at a time, and did the checker role help? (2) Which predictions were most often not supported, and did learners treat that as useful evidence rather than a mistake? (3) Did anyone say insulators have zero conduction or that doped silicon is charged, and was this corrected using the simulation evidence? (4) Were learners able to name at least one limit of the simulation compared with the real bulb test? (5) Did the group roles give quieter learners a chance to contribute, and were devices shared fairly? (6) Which new DQB questions point to Lesson 6 (superconductors and MRI) and Lesson 7 (solar panels, microchips and the Garissa solar plant)? Note what to revisit at the start of Lesson 6 based on the gallery walk question marks.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: What did the simulation show when we changed the energy gap (metal 0 eV, germanium 0.67 eV, silicon 1.1 eV, insulator above about 5 eV), raised the temperature of silicon, and added phosphorus or boron? Record the numbers and the number of free electrons and holes you saw.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: What did the simulation evidence tell us about how well our band model works? Which parts did it support, which parts did we have to change, and what are the limits of a simulation compared with the real bulb test in the Nairobi wiring circuit?
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Using the evidence, explain why copper lights the bulb while glass, wood and plastic almost do not, why silicon sits in between and conducts more when warmer, and how phosphorus (n-type) and boron (p-type) change it. Link your answer to why Mr Otieno can safely hold PVC-covered copper cable.

LESSONS.title: Superconductors and MRI Magnets: When Resistance Drops to Zero
LESSONS.aresKeywords: superconductor, critical temperature (Tc), zero resistance, Meissner effect, liquid nitrogen, YBCO, niobium-titanium (NbTi), MRI magnet, resistivity, class model

slo.purpose: Students extend the class model of resistance to current by investigating superconductors. They find that below the critical temperature a superconductor has zero resistance, and they use this to explain how MRI magnets work in hospitals such as Kenyatta National Hospital.
slo.knowledge: A superconductor is a material whose resistance drops to zero below its critical temperature (Tc). Mercury has Tc = 4.2 K (-269 C), niobium-titanium (NbTi) has Tc = 9.2 K and YBCO has Tc about 92 K (-181 C). Liquid nitrogen boils at 77 K (-196 C), which is below the Tc of YBCO, and liquid helium at 4.2 K cools NbTi. A YBCO disc cooled to 77 K levitates a magnet (Meissner effect). NbTi magnets in MRI machines carry large current without energy loss and give fields of about 1.5 T to 3 T. Copper, by comparison, has resistivity of 1.7 x 10^-8 ohm metre at about 20 C and its resistance rises slightly with temperature.
slo.skills: Developing and using models (revising the class model to show zero resistance); analysing and interpreting data (comparing Tc values with the 77 K and 4.2 K coolants); constructing explanations from evidence; obtaining, evaluating and communicating information (video or demonstration, Dr Wekesa's MRI case).
slo.attitudes: Curiosity about extreme-temperature materials; appreciation of how physics supports healthcare in Kenya; respect for others' ideas during discussion; responsibility when handling cryogenic liquids or watching the demonstration safely.
slo.keyInquiry: How do semiconductors and superconductors differ from ordinary conductors and insulators? How is electronics applied in day-to-day life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 1 to 5 explained why copper conducts, why plastic, glass and wood almost do not, and how semiconductors sit in between and can be doped. This lesson takes resistance to its extreme: some materials have none at all. It answers the part of the Driving Question about MRI machines and prepares students for the Lesson 7 case studies and final model-based answer.
slo.safetyNotes: Liquid nitrogen at 77 K (-196 C) causes severe cold burns and frostbite. ONLY the teacher (Ms Achieng) handles it, wearing safety goggles, insulated gloves and closed shoes, in a well-ventilated room, with students at least 2 m away. Never seal liquid nitrogen in a closed container. Use plastic tweezers for the YBCO disc and keep magnets away from phones and bank cards. If no liquid nitrogen is available, use the video demonstration instead. Students with pacemakers or implants should keep away from strong magnets. Keep the 3 V test circuit away from water.

LESSONS.overview: Back in Nairobi, Mr Otieno's copper cable carries current well, but even copper has some resistance, so some energy becomes heat. Wanjiku asks: 'Can any material have no resistance at all?' Students first predict what happens to the resistance of a metal as it gets very cold. Ms Achieng then runs the liquid nitrogen demonstration (or shows a video) of a YBCO disc cooled to 77 K levitating a magnet. Students compare the Tc values of mercury, NbTi and YBCO with the 77 K and 4.2 K coolants and explain Dr Wekesa's MRI magnet at Kenyatta National Hospital. They add zero resistance to the class model, add new questions to the Driving Question Board (DQB), and complete the summary table.

framework.learnerExperience: Students recall the Lesson 1 test circuit, in which copper made the bulb bright while glass, wood and plastic left it off, and the Lesson 2 resistivity of copper (1.7 x 10^-8 ohm metre). Wanjiku asks if a material could have no resistance. Individually, students draw a sketch graph of resistance against temperature for copper from 300 K down to 0 K and write one sentence predicting what happens to the resistance of a very cold metal. They then predict what will happen when a magnet is placed above a YBCO disc cooled in liquid nitrogen. They share in pairs.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the question: 'Mr Otieno's copper cable carries current, but does it carry it with zero resistance? What do you think happens if we cool a metal to very low temperatures?' Say: 'Sketch your own graph first. There is no wrong prediction today.' Give 2 minutes of silent drawing, then WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after asking for one volunteer. Cold-call 4 students (2 whose graph slopes to a small value, 2 whose graph drops to zero) and record predictions on the board without judging. Ask: 'What does resistance mean in our class model of electrons moving through copper?' and cold-call 2 more students.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain with a sketch graph: committing to a prediction in drawing exposes prior ideas (such as 'resistance just gets smaller slowly'), so students have a stake in the evidence they will see in the Observe Phase.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check the sketches: Does the student draw a graph with resistance falling with temperature (partial understanding), staying constant, or dropping abruptly to zero? Can the student link resistance to electrons colliding with atoms in the Lesson 1 model? Record the count of each prediction type on the board for comparison after the demonstration.

framework.learnerExperience: Students watch Ms Achieng's demonstration (or the video) of a YBCO disc at room temperature, with a small magnet that does not levitate. The disc is then cooled in liquid nitrogen at 77 K (-196 C) and the magnet floats above it (Meissner effect). Groups record observations in a table: temperature (K), whether the magnet levitates, and what happens as the disc warms above its Tc of about 92 K. Groups are then given a data card with: mercury Tc = 4.2 K (-269 C); NbTi Tc = 9.2 K; YBCO Tc about 92 K (-181 C); liquid nitrogen = 77 K; liquid helium = 4.2 K; copper resistivity 1.7 x 10^-8 ohm metre at about 20 C. They convert temperatures using K = C + 273 and mark which coolant works for each material. Finally, they watch a short clip or diagram of Dr Wekesa's MRI machine at a Nairobi hospital with a 1.5 T to 3 T magnet.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Everyone stand back at least 2 m. I am the only one handling the liquid nitrogen, because it is -196 C.' Pour with goggles and gloves and narrate: 'Watch the magnet. Write down exactly what you see, not what you think should happen.' After levitation, ask: 'What is different about the disc now compared to room temperature?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 students. Circulate while groups complete the data card, asking: 'Is 77 K above or below the Tc of YBCO? Is 77 K below the Tc of NbTi? So why does NbTi need liquid helium at 4.2 K?' Cold-call 3 groups to share their coolant matches. If no liquid nitrogen is available, play the video and pause at the levitation moment.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured data table with evidence-first observation: students separate observation (magnet floats below Tc, not above) from inference (resistance is zero), and converting units forces them to compare real numbers rather than rely on impressions.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: students record 'magnet floats only when the disc is below its Tc'; correctly convert -196 C to 77 K and -269 C to 4 K; state that 77 K is below the Tc of YBCO (about 92 K) but above the Tc of NbTi (9.2 K) and mercury (4.2 K). Note groups that wrongly say liquid nitrogen can cool NbTi into superconductivity and address this immediately.

framework.learnerExperience: Students revise their Predict graphs into a corrected graph: resistance falls gradually with temperature as for copper, then for a superconductor drops abruptly to zero at Tc. In groups they build an explanation of what zero resistance means for current: with zero resistance, current in a loop can flow without energy being lost as heat. They then answer: 'How does Dr Wekesa's MRI machine use NbTi?' using the data: a large current in NbTi coils creates a 1.5 T to 3 T field without energy loss, but only if the coils are kept at 4.2 K with liquid helium, below the Tc of 9.2 K. Using the Lesson 2 resistivity idea, they compare copper (1.7 x 10^-8 ohm metre, resistance that rises slightly with temperature) with a superconductor below Tc (zero). They write a Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) statement: 'A superconductor has zero resistance below Tc.' Students also discuss why household wiring still uses copper and PVC rather than superconductors.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Compare your Predict sketch to what we saw. What changed in your thinking?' Cold-call 4 students; WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before each. Ask: 'If the resistance is zero, where does the energy that would have become heat go?' and 'Why would Dr Wekesa's MRI magnet at Kenyatta National Hospital be very wasteful if it were made of copper?' Push for evidence: 'Which number on your data card supports that?' Ask: 'Why does Mr Otieno still use copper and PVC in the house?' Guide students to say that room temperature is far above every Tc listed (mercury 4.2 K, NbTi 9.2 K, YBCO about 92 K), so cooling would be needed. Correct: 'Superconductors are not the same as conductors; a superconductor has zero resistance only below Tc.' Cold-call 3 groups to read their CER aloud.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning with graph revision: students defend a claim with demonstration and data card evidence and connect it to the model of electrons and resistance from Lesson 1, so the explanation rests on the same mechanism rather than new facts.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for CER statements that: (claim) a superconductor has zero resistance below Tc; (evidence) the YBCO disc at 77 K levitates a magnet, 77 K is below its Tc of about 92 K; (reasoning) zero resistance allows large current with no energy lost as heat, so NbTi at 4.2 K gives 1.5 T to 3 T in MRI. Check that students use the terms conductor, superconductor and critical temperature correctly and do not call a superconductor an insulator.

framework.learnerExperience: Students revisit the class DQB kept by Wanjiku and Kamau. Using sticky notes, they mark questions answered by this lesson (e.g. 'Can any material have no resistance?'; 'How do MRI machines work?') and write new ones such as 'Why does YBCO levitate a magnet?' and 'Could we ever have a superconductor at room temperature for Kenyan power lines?' They sort the notes into 'Answered', 'Partly answered' and 'New'.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Go to the DQB. Which questions can we now answer with evidence from today? Which are new?' Give 3 minutes for writing, then WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds and cold-call 4 students to read one note and say which evidence supports their move. Ask: 'Which question will Lesson 7 help us answer, linking solar panels, microchips and MRI?' Point out the connection to the Driving Question about household wiring, solar panels, computers and MRI machines.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board sorting: tracking questions as answered, partly answered or new makes visible how evidence builds toward the Driving Question and keeps students' own curiosity driving the unit.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that at least 8 students add a new note, that questions are specific (mentioning Tc, MRI or YBCO), and that moved notes are justified with evidence from the demonstration or data card. Note students who ask about practical use, as they are ready for the Lesson 7 case studies.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups revise the class model of electrons, atoms and energy bands. They add a new panel for a superconductor below Tc: electrons move through the material with no resistance, shown as a smooth arrow with no collisions and no heat, beside the copper panel (electrons collide with atoms, slight resistance). They add temperature labels for Tc (mercury 4.2 K, NbTi 9.2 K, YBCO about 92 K) and a labelled sketch of an NbTi coil in an MRI machine at 4.2 K with liquid helium and a 1.5 T to 3 T magnetic field. Finally they complete the summary table (What we observed / What we learned / How we explain it).
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Add a superconductor panel to our class model. Show what is different from copper and from silicon. Use arrows and labels, and show the temperature.' Circulate and ask: 'Where on your model is the resistance? Why is the arrow smooth here?' and 'What would Dr Wekesa say happens if the NbTi warms above 9.2 K?' (resistance returns, so the magnet stops working). WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 groups to explain one feature. Remind them that the model still covers conductors (copper), insulators (glass, wood, plastic) and semiconductors (silicon, germanium, diode). Collect the summary tables as an exit check.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision: adding one new panel to the shared class model shows how zero resistance fits with the existing ideas, helping students see superconductors as a different case of the same electrons-and-resistance story.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: the model shows zero resistance below Tc with no energy lost as heat; Tc values and coolants (77 K nitrogen, 4.2 K helium) are labelled correctly; the MRI sketch links a large current in NbTi to a 1.5 T to 3 T field. Exit question: 'Why must the NbTi in Dr Wekesa's MRI machine stay at 4.2 K?' Look for the answer: it must stay below its Tc of 9.2 K to keep zero resistance.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, ask yourself: Did students separate what they saw (magnet floating below Tc) from what they inferred (zero resistance)? Did anyone confuse superconductors with ordinary conductors or think liquid nitrogen could make every material superconducting? Did temperature conversions (K = C + 273) slow groups down? Which students used evidence from the data card rather than recalled facts? If liquid nitrogen was unavailable and you used video, did students still engage with the levitation moment? What would you change about the questions on the DQB before Lesson 7?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed that a YBCO disc at room temperature did not levitate a magnet, but cooled to 77 K (-196 C) in liquid nitrogen it made the magnet float. We compared Tc values: mercury 4.2 K, NbTi 9.2 K, YBCO about 92 K, and noted which coolant (77 K or 4.2 K) is cold enough for each.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned that a superconductor has zero resistance below its critical temperature (Tc), unlike copper, which always has some resistance (1.7 x 10^-8 ohm metre at about 20 C). With zero resistance a large current flows with no energy lost as heat.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: We explain that Dr Wekesa's MRI machine uses NbTi coils cooled to 4.2 K with liquid helium, below the Tc of 9.2 K, so the magnet carries a large current without energy loss and gives a field of about 1.5 T to 3 T. Household wiring still uses copper and PVC because room temperature is far above every Tc we studied.

LESSONS.title: Case Studies and the Final Answer to the Driving Question
LESSONS.aresKeywords: conductor, insulator, semiconductor, superconductor, energy gap, doping, p-n junction, diode, critical temperature, class model, Driving Question Board (DQB)

slo.purpose: To apply all the ideas from Lessons 1 to 6 to three Kenyan technology cases (solar panels, microchips and superconducting MRI magnets), to compare the Lesson 1 class model with the final class model, and to write a final model-based answer to the Driving Question.
slo.knowledge: Learners explain that copper conducts because its outer electrons are free to move (bands overlap, 0 eV gap), while glass, wood and plastic have a large energy gap (above about 5 eV) so almost no electrons can move, making PVC a safe cover for wires. Silicon (1.1 eV) and germanium (0.67 eV) have a small gap, conduct a little, and conduct more when warmer. Doping with phosphorus (n-type) or boron (p-type) raises conductivity in a controlled way, and joining p and n gives a diode, the basis of solar panels and microchips. Superconductors below their critical temperature have zero resistance, so NbTi magnets in MRI machines carry large current without energy loss.
slo.skills: Analysing case studies; using evidence to develop and revise models (NGSS SEP 2); constructing explanations (NGSS SEP 6); engaging in argument from evidence (NGSS SEP 7); obtaining, evaluating and communicating information (NGSS SEP 8).
slo.attitudes: Appreciate the role of electronics in Kenya's technological growth (solar energy at Garissa, mobile money on phones, medical imaging at Kenyatta National Hospital). Show open-mindedness, respect for peers' ideas and responsibility when critiquing models.
slo.keyInquiry: 1. How do semiconductors and superconductors differ from ordinary conductors and insulators? 2. How is electronics applied in day-to-day life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: This is the final lesson of the storyline. Learners return to Mr Otieno's copper cable with its PVC cover and the five-material test (copper bright, glass, wood and plastic off, diode lit in one direction only). They use Lessons 1 to 6 evidence to finalise the class model, complete the Driving Question Board (DQB) and write the Final Explanation answering why some materials conduct while others do not and how this affects safety and efficiency in wiring, solar panels, computers and MRI machines.
slo.safetyNotes: This lesson is mostly discussion, case study reading and writing. If the 3 V test circuit (two 1.5 V dry cells, 3 V bulb, crocodile clips) is re-run for a quick recall, use only the dry cells, never mains 240 V. If the liquid nitrogen video is shown, make clear that liquid nitrogen (77 K, -196 C) is handled only by trained adults with goggles and gloves. Remind learners never to touch mains wiring, even when it appears insulated.

LESSONS.overview: Ms Achieng opens by asking learners to predict how the five-material results would be explained to Mr Otieno's client in Nairobi. Groups then work on one of three Kenyan case studies: the Garissa solar plant (50 MW, silicon p-n junctions), microchips in phones, M-Pesa and computers (silicon with billions of transistors), and the Kenyatta National Hospital MRI (NbTi magnets, zero resistance below Tc, field about 1.5 T to 3 T, Dr Wekesa). Learners use the class model, summary tables and posters from Lessons 1 to 6 as evidence. They compare the Lesson 1 model, which only showed electrons and atoms, with the final model that includes energy bands and gaps, free electrons, holes, doping and critical temperature. They complete the DQB by sorting questions as answered or still open, and each learner writes a Final Explanation that answers the Driving Question in their own words. Throughout, the language is conductor, insulator, semiconductor and superconductor, never mixed.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners look at the class poster of the five-material test (copper bright; glass, dry wood and plastic strip off; 1N4007 diode lit forward-connected and off reverse-connected). Individually they write 2 or 3 sentences predicting: 'If you had to explain to Mr Otieno why he can safely hold the PVC-covered copper cable at 240 V, which three ideas from our unit would you use?' They also predict which of the three Kenyan technologies (solar panel at Garissa, microchip in an M-Pesa phone, MRI magnet at Kenyatta National Hospital) uses a conductor, a semiconductor or a superconductor. They share with a partner.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the Lesson 1 class model and the five-material results. Say: 'Today we finish our story. Mr Otieno holds a live-looking cable safely. Before we look at any new evidence, write down which ideas you would use to explain that.' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before anyone writes. Walk around and note ideas. Cold-call 4 learners (not volunteers) to share one idea each. Then ask: 'Which of our three Kenyan cases uses a semiconductor? Which uses a superconductor? Turn and tell your partner.' Record predictions on the board without judging them. Say: 'We will check these against evidence in a few minutes.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain with Think-Pair-Share: writing a prediction first activates prior knowledge from Lessons 1 to 6 and makes learners accountable for their ideas. The shared record lets them later see how their thinking developed.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) learners who mention free electrons, energy gap or bands rather than only 'plastic does not allow electricity'; (2) learners who correctly match semiconductor to the solar panel and microchip and superconductor to the MRI magnet; (3) any learner who says insulators have zero conduction, or who mixes up conductor and semiconductor, to be addressed later. Tally on a class list how many of the 4 cold-called learners used the term energy gap.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners work in three expert groups, one per Kenyan case. Group A (Garissa solar plant, 50 MW; home solar kits): read the case card on silicon p-n junctions and identify the n-type (phosphorus) and p-type (boron) layers, and the role of the junction. Group B (microchips in phones, M-Pesa and computers): read about silicon chips with billions of transistors and why controlled doping and one-way behaviour (like the 1N4007 diode) matter. Group C (Kenyatta National Hospital MRI, Dr Wekesa): read about NbTi magnets (Tc 9.2 K) cooled by liquid helium at 4.2 K, field about 1.5 T to 3 T, zero resistance below Tc, with a short recap video or the YBCO levitation demonstration at 77 K (Meissner effect). Each group fills a 'Case Evidence Card' with three columns: material type (conductor, insulator, semiconductor or superconductor), property that matters, and what would go wrong without it. Then groups rotate in a jigsaw so each learner teaches their case to two others.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute case cards and the Evidence Card template. Say: 'Your job is to find out which kind of material does the key job in your case and which property from our class model explains it.' Circulate and ask: 'Which energy gap matters here?' 'Where in your case do you see the one-way action we saw with the diode?' 'Why does zero resistance mean no energy loss in the MRI magnet?' Allow WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each question. For Group C, remind: 'Superconductor means zero resistance only below Tc. NbTi needs 4.2 K; YBCO works at 77 K.' Cold-call 3 learners from different groups to state one fact from their card before the jigsaw. During the jigsaw, listen for correct vocabulary and gently correct any use of 'half conductor'. Also note that copper cable with PVC is a conductor plus insulator pair, to link back to Mr Otieno.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Jigsaw with case-based evidence gathering: every learner becomes responsible for one case and must teach it, which ensures all three applications are linked to the same underlying ideas (energy gap, doping, critical temperature). Using a common Evidence Card makes cross-case patterns visible.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check Evidence Cards for: Group A naming p-type (boron, holes) and n-type (phosphorus, electrons) layers and silicon as semiconductor; Group B stating that doping of about 1 atom in 10^7 to 10^8 controls conductivity and that the p-n junction conducts one way; Group C stating zero resistance below Tc, NbTi at 9.2 K cooled by helium at 4.2 K, and field about 1.5 T to 3 T. During the jigsaw, count how many learners can teach their case without reading from the card. Note learners who use 'free electrons', 'holes', 'forward-biased' correctly.

framework.learnerExperience: In mixed groups of four, learners build a 'Why does it work?' concept chain linking each case back to the phenomenon. They complete the sentence frames: 'Copper carries current in Mr Otieno's cable because ...', 'PVC makes the cable safe because ...', 'Silicon in a solar panel or chip is useful because ...', 'NbTi in the MRI magnet carries large current without energy loss because ...'. They then use the resistivity order (copper 1.7 x 10^-8 ohm metre, germanium 0.46, silicon 2.3 x 10^3, dry wood about 10^8 to 10^11, glass about 10^10 to 10^14, PVC about 10^13 or more) and energy gaps (metals 0 eV, germanium 0.67 eV, silicon 1.1 eV, insulators above about 5 eV) to justify the ranking. Finally each group prepares a 1-minute argument answering: 'Which one material property explains safety in wiring and efficiency in devices?'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Use evidence, not just words. Every claim needs a number or an observation from our unit.' Pose: 'Silicon is about 10^11 times more resistive than copper, yet it powers Garissa and your phone. How can both be true?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then ask groups to discuss for 2 minutes. Cold-call 3 groups to share, and ask a different group to agree, disagree or add evidence each time ('Who can build on that?'). Probe: 'What changes when we dope silicon?' 'What does the diode in our test circuit tell us about a solar cell?' 'Why is the PVC cover a good choice and not glass?' If a learner says insulators conduct nothing, respond: 'Say almost none. What does the large gap above about 5 eV do?' Do not re-teach lesson content; refer back to the class posters and summary tables instead.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) with peer argumentation: learners write a claim, back it with data from the posters and tables, and give reasoning with the energy band model. Peer challenge exposes gaps and strengthens explanations.
framework.formativeAssessment: Listen for reasoning that: links 0 eV gap (bands overlap) to free electrons in copper; links gap above about 5 eV to almost no moving electrons in PVC, wood and glass; explains that doping greatly raises silicon conductivity in a controlled way and the p-n junction gives one-way conduction; explains zero resistance below Tc as no energy lost as heat. Use a quick checklist of these four points per group. Flag misconceptions such as 'doped silicon is charged' (it remains electrically neutral overall) or 'superconductors work at room temperature'.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revisit the class DQB, which has been kept by Wanjiku and Kamau's class throughout the unit. In pairs they take the question sticky notes and sort them into three groups: 'Answered with evidence', 'Partly answered', and 'New or still open questions'. For each answered question they attach the evidence source (for example the five-material test, resistivity table, doping explanation, PhET simulation, liquid nitrogen demonstration or video). Each learner then adds one new question that could be investigated next, such as 'Can we make solar panels cheaper in Kenya?' or 'Could a superconductor work at room temperature?'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Our board started with puzzles. Let us see how many we can now answer, and what evidence supports each answer.' Hand out the sticky notes and allow WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before pairs begin sorting. Circulate and ask: 'Which lesson gave you the evidence for this answer?' Cold-call 4 pairs to place one question and justify where it belongs. Ask the class: 'Which questions are still open, and why does that make science exciting?' Make sure the two KICD key inquiry questions are visible and answered: how semiconductors and superconductors differ from ordinary conductors and insulators, and how electronics is applied in day-to-day life. Photograph the completed DQB for the record.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: DQB sorting with evidence tagging: connecting each answered question to a specific piece of evidence shows how knowledge was built over the unit, and marking open questions models how scientists keep asking.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that at least most of the DQB questions are correctly placed and that each 'Answered' note names a valid evidence source. Look for learners who write new questions that extend ideas (for example about cost, temperature, efficiency or safety) rather than repeat old ones. Note pairs who cannot link a question to a lesson for follow-up.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners compare the Lesson 1 class model (electrons and atoms with the puzzle of why materials differ) to the final class model. Individually they draw a final model on A4 paper or in their exercise book showing: energy bands with the gap for a metal like copper (0 eV, bands overlap), a semiconductor such as silicon (1.1 eV) and germanium (0.67 eV), and an insulator such as glass or PVC (above about 5 eV); n-type (phosphorus, extra free electrons) and p-type (boron, holes) silicon; the p-n junction in a diode; and a note on superconductors below Tc. They add arrows or labels showing where each fits in Kenyan cases: Mr Otieno's PVC-covered copper cable, Garissa solar plant, microchips, and the Kenyatta National Hospital MRI. Then each learner writes their Final Explanation answering the Driving Question: 'Why do some materials conduct electricity while others do not, and how does this affect the safety and efficiency of household wiring and of devices such as solar panels, computers and MRI machines?' Use the sentence starters: 'Copper conducts because ...', 'Glass, wood and plastic ...', 'Silicon and germanium ...', 'Superconductors ...'. Pairs swap and give one 'glow' and one 'grow' comment before final edits.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the Lesson 1 model beside a blank space for the final one. Say: 'Look at our first model. What could it not explain? What can our final model explain now?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners to name one thing the final model explains better. Remind learners that doped silicon is electrically neutral and that insulators have almost none, not zero, conduction. While they draw and write, circulate with a checklist and prompt: 'Where is the energy gap in your drawing?' 'Which carriers are the majority in p-type?' 'How does your model explain why Mr Otieno can hold the insulated wire safely?' Share the exemplar outcome statement only after learners have drafted their own: copper conducts because its outer electrons are free to move through the metal; glass, wood and plastic have a large gap above about 5 eV so almost no electrons move, which makes plastic a safe cover; silicon and germanium have small gaps and conduct a little, more when warmer, and doping with phosphorus or boron greatly raises conductivity in a controlled way; joining p and n gives a diode that conducts one way only, the basis of solar panels and microchips; superconductors below Tc have zero resistance so NbTi magnets in MRI machines carry large current without energy loss. Learners then compare it with their draft and revise.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Model revision and comparison (before and after) combined with a written Final Explanation: contrasting the Lesson 1 model with the final model makes the growth in understanding explicit, and writing the explanation in their own words consolidates the cause-and-effect reasoning from energy gap to function.
framework.formativeAssessment: Use a rubric with four observable indicators: (1) the model correctly shows gaps in order metals 0 eV, germanium 0.67 eV, silicon 1.1 eV, insulators above about 5 eV; (2) shows n-type with free electrons and p-type with holes, and the one-way p-n junction; (3) mentions zero resistance of superconductors below Tc with NbTi in MRI; (4) the Final Explanation links properties to safety (PVC cover) and efficiency (copper wiring, solar, chips, MRI) using correct vocabulary and Kenyan examples. Record learners who meet at least 3 indicators and plan support for others.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, ask: Did learners use evidence from earlier lessons (the five-material test, resistivity order, energy gaps, doping, Tc values) instead of memorised statements? Which learners still confuse semiconductors with superconductors or say insulators conduct zero? Were all three Kenyan cases (Garissa solar plant, microchips, Kenyatta National Hospital MRI) understood as applications of the same ideas? How did the final model differ from the Lesson 1 model in each learner's work? Did the Final Explanation answer both parts of the Driving Question, safety and efficiency? Which DQB questions remain open and could become project work or career talks (electrician, radiographer, solar technician, electronics engineer)? Note adjustments for the next class, including more time for model drawing or a repeat of the liquid nitrogen video if needed.

In the Kenyan cases we saw silicon p-n junctions at work in the Garissa solar plant (50 MW) and in microchips, and an NbTi superconducting magnet cooled to 4.2 K in the Kenyatta National Hospital MRI, with a YBCO disc levitating a magnet at 77 K.

FINAL_EXPLANATION.instructions: This is your Final Explanation. Use your own words to answer the Driving Question: Why do some materials conduct electricity while others do not, and how does this affect the safety and efficiency of household wiring and of devices such as solar panels, computers and MRI machines? Use the evidence from your five-material bulb test, the resistivity data, your class model, the Driving Question Board (DQB) and the Kenyan case studies. Write your answers in the space under each prompt. Use the words conductor, insulator, semiconductor and superconductor carefully, and give numbers and units where you can. Show your thinking in full sentences. Use the data table in Section 2 when it is asked for.

sections.title: Section 1: What the five-material test showed
sections.prompt:
Mr Otieno, an electrician in Nairobi, wires a house with copper cable covered in PVC plastic and can safely hold the insulated wire while it carries current at 240 V. In class you tested copper wire, glass, dry wood, plastic and a silicon diode (1N4007) in a 3 V circuit with a torch bulb, always in that order.
(a) Describe what happened to the bulb for each of the five materials, including both ways of connecting the diode.
(b) How many of the four ordinary materials (copper, glass, wood, plastic) let the bulb light? What was different about the diode?
(c) Use your results to explain why Mr Otieno can safely hold the plastic-covered copper cable.
sections.exemplar:
(a) Copper wire: the bulb was bright. Glass: the bulb was off. Dry wood: the bulb was off. Plastic strip: the bulb was off. Silicon diode (1N4007): the bulb lit when it was forward-connected (forward-biased) and was off when it was reverse-connected (reverse-biased).
(b) Only 1 of the 4 ordinary materials, copper, let the bulb light. The diode was different from all of them because it conducts in one direction only.
(c) Copper is a conductor, so it carries current easily along the wire. Plastic (PVC) is an insulator that lets almost no current through, so the current stays inside the copper and almost none passes to Mr Otieno's hand. This makes the plastic cover a safe layer for the cable even at 240 V.  Insulators allow almost no current, not exactly none.

sections.title: Section 2: Using resistivity data to classify materials
sections.prompt:
The table shows approximate resistivity values at about 20 C.

| Material | Resistivity rho (ohm metre) |
| --- | --- |
| Copper | 1.7 x 10^-8 |
| Germanium (pure) | 0.46 |
| Silicon (pure) | 2.3 x 10^3 |
| Dry wood | about 10^8 to 10^11 |
| Glass | about 10^10 to 10^14 |
| PVC | about 10^13 or more |

(a) Put the materials in order from best to worst conductor.
(b) Sort them into conductor, semiconductor and insulator.
(c) Calculate how many times more resistive pure silicon is than copper. Show your working.
(d) How is conductivity related to resistivity?
(e) Use the data to explain why household wiring uses copper covered in PVC.
sections.exemplar:
(a) Best to worst conductor (lowest to highest resistivity): copper, germanium, silicon, dry wood, then glass and PVC (the highest).
(b) Conductor: copper. Semiconductors: germanium and silicon. Insulators: dry wood, glass and PVC.
(c) Silicon / copper = (2.3 x 10^3) / (1.7 x 10^-8) = about 1.4 x 10^11. Silicon is about 1.4 x 10^11 times (about 10^11 times) more resistive than copper.
(d) Conductivity is the reciprocal of resistivity: conductivity = 1/rho.
(e) Copper has a very low resistivity (1.7 x 10^-8 ohm metre), so it carries current efficiently with little energy wasted. PVC has a very high resistivity (about 10^13 ohm metre or more), so it allows almost no current to leave the wire. Together they make wiring efficient and safe for people to handle.

sections.title: Section 3: Why materials differ: energy gaps, temperature and doping
sections.prompt:
All the materials you tested are made of atoms with electrons, yet they behave very differently.
(a) Using the idea of energy bands and the energy gap (Eg), explain why copper conducts but glass, wood and plastic almost do not. Give the gap values you used.
(b) Why does pure (intrinsic) silicon conduct a little, and what are the holes that appear? How does warming change its conductivity? How is this different from copper?
(c) Explain how doping silicon with phosphorus and with boron changes its conduction. Name the type of semiconductor and the majority carriers in each case. Is doped silicon charged?
(d) Why is doping useful, and how does a p-n junction explain the result you saw with the diode and the bulb?
sections.exemplar:
(a) In copper (a metal) the bands overlap, so the energy gap is 0 eV and outer electrons are free to move through the metal as free electrons. In glass, wood and plastic the energy gap is large (above about 5 eV), so almost no electrons gain enough energy to move, and almost no current flows.
(b) Pure silicon has a small gap (1.1 eV; germanium 0.67 eV). At room temperature a few electrons gain enough energy to cross the gap and become free electrons. Each leaves behind a hole (a missing electron), making an electron-hole pair. Warming makes more pairs, so the conductivity of silicon rises. In copper, the resistance rises slightly when warmed.
(c) Phosphorus has 5 valence electrons, so it adds an extra free electron: n-type, majority carriers electrons. Boron has 3 valence electrons, so it leaves a hole: p-type, majority carriers holes. Doped silicon is still electrically neutral overall.
(d) Typical doping is about 1 atom in 10^7 to 10^8, which raises conductivity by a factor of many thousands, so conduction can be controlled. Joining p-type and n-type gives a p-n junction (a diode), which conducts when forward-biased (bulb lit) and blocks current when reverse-biased (bulb off).

sections.title: Section 4: Superconductors and MRI machines
sections.prompt:
Ms Achieng showed a YBCO disc cooled in liquid nitrogen at 77 K (-196 C) making a magnet float. The critical temperatures (Tc) are: mercury 4.2 K, NbTi 9.2 K, YBCO about 92 K.
(a) What is special about the resistance of a superconductor below its Tc, and how is this different from copper?
(b) Dr Wekesa operates an MRI machine at Kenyatta National Hospital. Which coolant (liquid nitrogen at 77 K or liquid helium at 4.2 K) is needed for the NbTi magnet? Explain using the data.
(c) Why does an MRI magnet need a superconductor, and why is household wiring still copper and PVC?
sections.exemplar:
(a) Below its critical temperature (Tc) a superconductor has zero resistance. Copper always has some resistance (1.7 x 10^-8 ohm metre at about 20 C), so some energy always becomes heat.
(b) Liquid helium at 4.2 K is needed. NbTi has Tc = 9.2 K, and 4.2 K is below 9.2 K, but liquid nitrogen at 77 K is far above 9.2 K, so NbTi would not be superconducting. (YBCO, with Tc about 92 K, works at 77 K.)
(c) With zero resistance, the NbTi coils carry a very large current without energy lost as heat, giving the strong magnetic field of about 1.5 T to 3 T. Household wiring stays copper and PVC because room temperature is far above every Tc we studied.

sections.title: Section 5: Final answer to the Driving Question
sections.exemplar:
Materials differ in whether they let current flow because of their energy bands. In copper the bands overlap (gap 0 eV), so its outer electrons are free to move, and its resistivity is very low (1.7 x 10^-8 ohm metre). In glass, wood and plastic the gap is above about 5 eV, so almost no electrons can move and resistivity is very high (PVC about 10^13 ohm metre or more). In our bulb test, only copper out of the four ordinary materials lit the bulb. This is why Mr Otieno's Nairobi wiring uses copper for efficient current flow and PVC as an insulator, so he can safely hold the cable at 240 V.
Silicon and germanium are semiconductors with small gaps (1.1 eV and 0.67 eV), so a few free electrons and holes form and they conduct a little, more when warmer. Doping with phosphorus (n-type) or boron (p-type), about 1 atom in 10^7 to 10^8, raises conductivity thousands of times in a controlled way. A p-n junction conducts one way only (our diode lit the bulb forward-biased and not reverse-biased). This is the basis of silicon solar panels such as the 50 MW Garissa solar plant and of the microchips with billions of transistors in phones, M-Pesa and computers.
Superconductors have zero resistance below their critical temperature. At Kenyatta National Hospital, the MRI uses NbTi coils (Tc 9.2 K) cooled to 4.2 K by liquid helium, so large current flows without energy loss and gives a field of about 1.5 T to 3 T.

lessons.title: Classifying Conductors, Insulators and Semiconductors

lessons.title: Intrinsic Semiconductors: Silicon and Germanium
lessons.observed: We observed that the silicon diode (1N4007) forward-connected lit the 3 V bulb, as in Lesson 1, and that the data show silicon (rho about 2.3 x 10^3 ohm metre) and germanium (about 0.46 ohm metre) are far more resistive than copper (1.7 x 10^-8 ohm metre) but far less than glass. lessons.learned: We learned that pure (intrinsic) silicon and germanium have a small energy gap (1.1 eV and 0.67 eV), so at room temperature a few electrons gain enough energy to become free electrons, each leaving a hole to make an electron-hole pair. lessons.explained: We explained that silicon conducts a little because its small gap lets a few electrons cross, unlike glass, wood and PVC with a gap above about 5 eV that allow almost no free electrons, and unlike copper, where the bands overlap. lessons.title: Doping: Making n-type and p-type Semiconductors
lessons.observed: We re-tested the 1N4007 diode: the bulb lit when it was forward-connected (forward-biased) and stayed off when it was reverse-connected (reverse-biased). lessons.explained: Pure silicon conducts very poorly (resistivity about 2.3 x 10^3 ohm metre), but a tiny amount of phosphorus or boron adds free electrons or holes, so conductivity rises thousands of times in a controlled way. A p-n junction lets current pass when forward-biased (bulb lit) and blocks it when reverse-biased (bulb off), which is why doped silicon is the basis of diodes, solar panels like those at Garissa, and microchips in phones and computers.
